claim: The best published learned coach-vs-student comparison result in this source is modest. On a subject-disjoint test set, the exemplar-comparison model's predicted 0-100 technique scores reach MAE 7.47, RMSE 9.09, SRCC 0.56 and PLCC 0.58 against expert coach scores. 38% of predictions fall within 5 points and 73% within 10 points. The paper reports no other baselines, such as DTW alignment or pose and joint-angle comparison, so the comparison method the app uses now cannot be compared directly.
quote: Overall Performance 7.47 9.09 0.56 0.58 38% 73% ... the model achieves an MAE of 7.47 and an RMSE of 9.09 ... the SRCC and PLCC coefficients reach 0.56 and 0.58 respectively ... the model attains Acc05 of 38% and Acc10 of 73%

claim: The benchmark is a smartphone-captured badminton technique-assessment dataset. It has 7,200 clips covering 10 fundamental strokes (forehand/backhand clear, serve, lift, net drop and drive) from 5 professional coaches and 67 university students. Students are scored on a 100-point scale by several coaches, with the highest and lowest scores dropped. The split is by student: 53 students for training and 14 for testing. The data is available only on request.
quote: The dataset contains 7,200 smartphone-captured video clips covering 10 fundamental badminton strokes, collected from 5 professional coaches and 67 university students across multiple real-world scenarios. Student performances are annotated on a 100-point scale by expert coaches using a multi-rater scoring protocol.

claim: The baseline compares RGB appearance, not skeletons. It uses a pretrained ViT on each frame (only 8 sampled frames at 224x224), then self-attention temporal fusion with mean pooling. Coach and student features are compared by subtraction plus bilinear pooling, followed by a linear regression head trained with RMSE loss. It was trained on an NVIDIA 4090 GPU, and the paper gives no mobile latency figures.
quote: we compute the overall discrepancy between the exemplar and student features via a subtraction operation ... we employ the following bilinear pooling operation to capture the local discrepancies ... the input video frames are resized to 224 × 224 pixels ... the number of sampled frames T for each video is set to 8

claim: How well the model agrees with coaches depends strongly on the stroke. Overhead and forehand strokes are hardest: Forehand Clear has SRCC 0.32 / PLCC 0.34 and MAE 8.90, and Forehand Serve has SRCC 0.34. Drives and the backhand serve do best: Backhand Drive has SRCC 0.75 / PLCC 0.75 and MAE 6.04.
quote: Forehand Clear 8.90 11.11 0.32 0.34 34% 64% ... Backhand Drive 6.04 7.27 0.75 0.75 46% 82% ... the prediction performance on the remaining 2 strokes, namely Forehand Clear and Forehand Serve, is relatively inferior

claim: Clips were recorded with handheld phones and phones on fixed holders, in places other than courts (dormitories, teaching buildings). This matches the single-phone capture conditions of a consumer app, not lab or multi-camera setups.
quote: data acquisition is performed in two modes: fixed shooting with a smartphone holder and handheld shooting ... we require students to perform the technical movements in different scenarios, including dormitories and teaching buildings, rather than being limited to badminton courts only.

claim: For action recognition on unseen motion categories, learned deep metric approaches, including the proposed MMD-NCA loss with an attentive BiLSTM, cut false positive rate by up to 17% relative to DTW-family measures (DTW, MDDTW, CTW, GDTW). Table 1 on CMU mocap gives FPR at 70% TPR of 20.29 for MMD-NCA against 37.62 for DTW. On Human3.6M the figures are 33.13 against 44.38. This supports replacing hand-crafted per-joint or DTW comparison with a learned similarity embedding, but the benchmark measures action-category similarity, not fine-grained technique quality within one stroke type.
quote: With a true positive rate of 70%, the learning approaches [33,41,45,35] including our approach achieve up to 17% improvement in FPR relative to DTW [42], MDDTW [25], CTW [47] and GDTW [48].

claim: DTW fails when the distinctive pose fills only a short part of a long sequence, because the non-informative frames dominate the distance. In a cartwheel retrieval query on CMU mocap, DTW returned jumping, laughing and standing motions. This matters for badminton technique comparison, where the stroke-defining moment (backswing to contact) is brief within a longer clip.
quote: DTW [42] fails to match the query to the dataset because the distinctive pose appears on a small portion of the sequence. This implies that the large portion, where the actor stands, dominates the similarity measure.

claim: On motion-based person identification (CMU mocap, 29 unseen test subjects, 64-d embedding), MMD-NCA beats DTW-based measures by about 20% and other deep metric losses (Triplet, Triplet+GOR, N-Pair, DCTW) by about 2%. Table 2 gives FPR at 70% TPR of 2.55 for MMD-NCA against 22.85 for DTW. This suggests learned embeddings capture an individual's movement style, which is relevant to comparing a user's style against a pro's.
quote: our method outperforms all the approaches for all FPR with a 20% improvement against DTW [42], MDDTW [25], CTW [47] and GDTW [48], and a 2% improvement compared to the state-of-the-art deep learning approaches

claim: In the ablation, self-attention over the pose sequence is the most important architectural component. Removing it causes the largest drop in NMI and F1. Layer normalization improves FPR by about 7% and self-attention by about 10%. The attention also learns to focus on the key action frame (for example, the ball-throw moment in basketball sequences).
quote: Notably, the removal of the self-attention mechanism yields the biggest drop in NMI and F1 on all the datasets. In addition, Both the layer normalization and the self-attention improve the resulting FPR by 7% and 10%, respectively.

claim: The evaluation covers only clean 3D motion-capture data (CMU mocap, Human3.6M), aligned to the torso, in exponential-map representation and downsampled to 30 Hz. It includes no monocular 2D pose estimates, no sports or racket data, and no on-device latency. Transfer to noisy smartphone BlazePose keypoints of fast badminton strokes is therefore unverified by this paper.
quote: We tested the models on two different datasets: (1) the CMU Graphics Lab motion capture database (CMU mocap) [1]; and, (2) the Human3.6M dataset [17].

claim: Morel et al. (VISAPP 2016) compare a learner's motion with a model built only from expert recordings, with no hand-coded rules. They use a 2-level DTW: one DTW aligns the whole body, then a separate DTW aligns each joint. This gives a spatial error and a temporal (timing) error for every joint at every time step. It is a direct alternative to the app's current per-joint angle comparison for stage 7.
quote: Only based on a database of experts' motions and no additional knowledge, we propose an innovative 2-level DTW (Dynamic Time Warping) approach to temporally and spatially align the motions and extract the imperfections of the novice's performance for each joints.

claim: The authors argue that one whole-body DTW gives only a single overall error score. It cannot show which joint is wrong or detect timing problems between limbs. Aligning each joint on its own loses the links between joints. The 2-level design is meant to fix both problems.
quote: Actually, a single DTW can only give information about the global error of the motion without considering the temporality between limbs for instance and without localizing the errors. Another solution could have been to manage each joint independently but no relationships between the joints could then be identified.

claim: How the expert model is built: every expert trial is DTW-aligned to the longest trial and averaged into a mean trajectory. Allowed spatial variation is stored as a 3x3 covariance matrix per joint per time step, and allowed timing variation as a standard deviation. The DTW cost uses both joint positions and their derivatives (derivative DTW). Before alignment, poses are centred on the root joint, rotated to face the hips' direction, and scaled by the head-to-root distance so body size matters less. A learner's spatial error is the Mahalanobis distance from the expert mean under that covariance.
quote: the spatial errors are computed with the Mahalanobis distances between the trajectories of the novice's motion x̃a(t) and of the model of experts xamean(t) where ΣS(t, a) is a 3 × 3 matrix modeling the spatial tolerance

claim: The evidence is small and weak. Data came from a Vicon MX-40 optical marker system (43 markers, 25 3D joint centres), not from monocular phone video. The sport was the tennis serve, not badminton. There were 9 expert players (women aged 14-18) and 2 novices, giving 79 expert and 20 novice trials. Results are shown only as box plots in which expert and novice errors look separated. No classification accuracy figure is reported, and the authors call the results preliminary.
quote: we captured the tennis serves of 9 experts (14-18 year old women) and 2 novice players. Each of them made 8 to 10 examples (or trials) leading to a database of 79 expert and 20 novice examples ... these preliminary results must be extended to a bigger population to have a statistical analysis.

claim: To find the global alignment, the method repeatedly picks random subsets of joints, in the style of RANSAC (N_RANSAC=50 rounds, 5 joints per subset, threshold kT=3). This stops one badly timed joint from distorting the alignment. The authors note that it also makes the output random, so repeated runs can give different results. In the worked example, the novice's right elbow had a temporal error of 50.48 at the moment of ball impact, which the authors read as the arm moving too early.
quote: Our algorithm is based on a random-based selection process that could make it stochastic and then subject to variations. On the contrary, this process allows the detection of outliers, i.e. joints that are badly synchronized with others, in an efficient way.

claim: Drop-DTW extends standard DTW so that it aligns only the signal two sequences share and drops outlier elements interspersed anywhere in either sequence, including at the endpoints. Matching and dropping are solved together in one dynamic program, and a smooth-min relaxation makes it differentiable, so it can be used as a training loss. For Ayto's pro comparison, this means a user's stroke clip that contains irrelevant frames (idle, footwork, occlusion) could be aligned to a pro reference without forcing every frame to match.
quote: we introduce Drop-DTW, a novel algorithm that aligns the common signal between the sequences while automatically dropping the outlier elements from the matching. The entire procedure is implemented as a single dynamic program that is efficient and fully differentiable.

claim: Used purely at inference on the same frozen embeddings, Drop-DTW beat every other alignment algorithm tested on all three datasets. Accuracy / IoU on CrossTask: Drop-DTW 70.2 / 30.5; DTW 11.2 / 10.1; OTAM 19.5 / 11.6; LCSS 50.3 / 4.1; Needleman-Wunsch 68.8 / 9.5; greedy drop + DTW 60.1 / 13.8. On YouCook2: Drop-DTW 66.0 / 47.5 vs DTW 35.0 / 31.1.
quote: Table 2 demonstrates that Drop-DTW outperforms all the existing methods on all metrics and datasets by a significant margin. This is due to their inability to drop interspersed outliers or due to their restricted space of possible matches.

claim: In a controlled retrieval test (TMNIST, Recall@1, query frames randomly blurred as noise), plain DTW was very sensitive to the interspersed noise. At the highest noise level, Drop-DTW (constant drop cost 0.3, no training) scored 8x better than DTW.
quote: As expected, DTW is very sensitive to interspersed noise. In contrast, Drop-DTW remains robust across the range of noise levels. Concretely, for the highest noise level in Fig 3(a), we see that Drop-DTW is 8× better than DTW

claim: On PennAction, a dataset of human sport and action videos (e.g., baseball pitch and swing), the authors added 0-70% outlier frames taken from other actions. Embeddings trained with the Drop-DTW loss gave better video alignment (Kendall's Tau) than those trained with SmoothDTW, a soft-min differentiable DTW, and held up better as the outlier rate rose. This suggests it can learn alignment-based motion similarity for sport actions.
quote: Fig. 5 demonstrates the strong performance of Drop-DTW as a loss for representation learning, which once again proves to be more resilient to outliers.

claim: The drop cost can be set per instance as the p-th top percentile of the match-cost matrix, which encodes a prior on the expected outlier rate. It can also be learned by a small feed-forward network. Drop-DTW still enforces a monotonic (strictly ordered) alignment, so it cannot handle signals whose phases are only partially ordered.
quote: the final alignment is still subject to the monotonicity constraint, which is based on the assumption that the relevant signals are strictly ordered.

claim: A smartphone badminton smash-speed system that combines a custom YOLOv5 shuttle detector with a linear constant-velocity Kalman filter (a SORT-style setup, close to Ayto's current YOLOv8n+KF approach) produced peak speeds far from radar: MAE 66.41 km/h and RMSE 74.68 km/h over 20 smashes filmed on an iPhone 16 at 30 FPS against a Bushnell Speedster III radar. The system's peak readings ran well above radar in every trial (for example, 214.6 vs 132.0 km/h).
quote: The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between the two methods for peak speed was 66.41 km/h, and the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) was 74.68 km/h.

claim: Speed was taken at the net crossing instead of at the peak, and these readings were much closer to radar. The paper gives no MAE for this. Computed from its Table 1, the at-net MAE is about 9.9 km/h, with the worst trials off by about 31 to 34 km/h (trial 5: 178.2 vs 144.0; trial 15: 118.0 vs 87.0).
quote: the at-net readings "align remarkably well" with the radar

claim: Court calibration needs no homography or keypoint detection. The user clicks two points on a court line at the same depth as the impact point, and the system computes one meters-per-pixel scale factor (S_f = d_real / d_pixel). This strictly 2D planar method cannot measure cross-court or angled smashes correctly and underestimates speed for any motion toward or away from the camera.
quote: the strict 2D planar assumption means the system cannot accurately measure the speed of cross-court smashes

claim: The custom YOLOv5 shuttle detector reached precision 93%, recall 87% and mAP@0.5 of 91%. It was trained on 15,000 annotated images, all from a perpendicular side view, and ran at a low confidence threshold of 0.1 with IoU 0.45.
quote: Upon completion of training, the model achieved a precision of 93%, a recall of 87%, and a mean Average Precision at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (mAP@0.5) of 91%.

claim: Candidates were chosen with a composite score of 0.3 x YOLO confidence + 0.7 x Kalman-prediction proximity, with weights set empirically. Detections implying speeds below 5 km/h or above 375 km/h were rejected. No on-device FPS or latency was reported, and validation was limited to 20 sub-maximal smashes by one player.
quote: Validation used only 20 smashes, kept "below maximum power due to the radar gun's limitations."

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1); revised v2 2025-10-24 (formatted for IEEE Transactions on Image Processing; authors from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
claim: HP-MCoRe scores a performance relative to a reference: it predicts the query video's quality score from the gap between the query and an exemplar video whose score is known, using both the videos and their skeleton sequences. At inference it averages over N=10 sampled exemplars. This is a learned, exemplar-relative similarity and scoring method, an alternative to per-joint angle or DTW comparison against a pro reference. Its backbones are heavy (I3D, ResNetY, HD-GCN, Transformer decoder) and the paper reports no mobile latency, so it suits cloud post-processing rather than on-device use.
quote: Given a pair of query video V^q and exemplar video V^e, along with their respective skeletal sequences P^q and P^e, the object is to predict quality score Ŝ^q of V^q based on the quality score S^e of V^e

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1); revised v2 2025-10-24 (formatted for IEEE Transactions on Image Processing; authors from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
claim: On FineDiving, HP-MCoRe reports SRCC 0.9041 and R-L2(x100) 0.411 without dive-number labels, and SRCC 0.9383 and R-L2 0.269 with them. Both beat the prior baselines it lists: MCoRe at 0.8897/0.461 and 0.9232/0.326, and TSA at 0.8925/0.478 and 0.9203/0.342. On MTL-AQA it reports SRCC 0.9266 without difficulty labels, which is best, and 0.9516 with them, second behind TPT at 0.9552.
quote: Specifically, our method achieved an SRCC of 0.9041 and an R_L2 of 0.411 without using dive numbers. When dive numbers are incorporated, the SRCC improves to 0.9383 and the R_L2 reduces to 0.269.

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1); revised v2 2025-10-24 (formatted for IEEE Transactions on Image Processing; authors from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
claim: Splitting the motion into sub-action phases dynamically, with a learned Bi-GRU segmenter, works better than fixed-length clips. Stage-boundary AIoU@0.5/0.75 is 99.07/97.96, against 82.51/34.31 for TSA. In the ablation, SRCC rises from 0.9247 with 1 stage to 0.9383 with 3 stages (take-off, flight, entry). This suggests that comparing a stroke against a pro reference phase by phase (e.g. preparation, swing, follow-through) should beat comparing whole sequences.
quote: existing methods focus on segmenting the video into fixed frames, which disrupts the temporal continuity of sub-actions resulting in unavoidable prediction errors

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1); revised v2 2025-10-24 (formatted for IEEE Transactions on Image Processing; authors from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
claim: Skeleton features alone are much weaker than visual+skeleton fusion for judging movement quality. The hierarchical skeletal encoder alone reaches SRCC 0.6847, the dynamic visual encoder alone 0.8914, and the full fused model 0.9383. Adding the skeletal encoder to the visual encoder gives a 3.57% SRCC gain. This means pose-only comparison, like the app's per-joint angles, leaves accuracy on the table.
quote: utilizing the HSE alone results in inferior performance, with an SRCC of 0.6847

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1); revised v2 2025-10-24 (formatted for IEEE Transactions on Image Processing; authors from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
claim: Off-the-shelf HRNet pose estimation degrades on fast, motion-blurred athletic footage. The authors built FineDiving-Pose (12,722 manually labeled frames and 288,000 auto-labeled frames) and fine-tuned HRNet on it to get reliable keypoints. This points to the need for domain fine-tuning of pose models on fast sports motion.
quote: HRNet struggles to estimate the precise human pose, due to the poor image quality resulting from high-speed motions and extreme body distortions.

published: 2024-03-25 (arXiv v2; accepted to International Journal of Computer Vision 25.03.2024)
claim: JEANIE extends soft-DTW (a differentiable form of DTW) by aligning 3D skeleton sequences over time and camera viewpoint together. It matches support and query temporal blocks across neighbouring time indices and adjacent simulated camera views, then uses a soft-minimum to pick the lowest-distance path. Plain DTW and soft-DTW align time only. For Ayto's pro-comparison stage, this means soft-DTW is the established differentiable baseline, and adding viewpoint alignment is the documented extension.
quote: By the use of soft-minimum, the path with the minimum aggregated distance is selected as the output of JEANIE. Thus, while DTW provides optimal temporal alignment of support-query sequence pairs, JEANIE simultaneously provides the optimal joint temporal-viewpoint alignment.

published: 2024-03-25 (arXiv v2; accepted to International Journal of Computer Vision 25.03.2024)
claim: In the paper's own experiments on skeleton few-shot action recognition, unsupervised JEANIE beats temporal-only soft-DTW by up to 5% on NTU-60, 9% on NTU-120 and 6% on Kinetics-skeleton. The largest gain, about 10%, is on UWA3D Multiview Activity II, the dataset with heavy camera-pose variation.
quote: unsupervised JEANIE (temporal-viewpoint alignment) outperforms soft-DTW (temporal alignment only) by up to 5%, 9% and 6% on NTU-60, NTU-120 and Kinetics-skeleton, respectively. Table 8 (Unsup.) shows that the biggest improvement is obtained when using unsupervised JEANIE on UWA3D Multiview Activity II dataset, with 10% performance gain.

published: 2024-03-25 (arXiv v2; accepted to International Journal of Computer Vision 25.03.2024)
claim: In supervised few-shot recognition on NTU-60 (Table 5, 10 to 50 training classes), soft-DTW gets 53.7/56.2/60.0/63.9/67.8% accuracy and no alignment (S2GC backbone) gets 50.8/54.7/58.8/60.2/62.8%. JEANIE with CamVPC viewpoint simulation gets 59.7/68.7/68.4/70.4/73.2%, rising to 63.4/72.4/73.5/73.2/78.1% with cross-validation. Temporal alignment alone adds a few points, and joint temporal-viewpoint alignment adds more.

published: 2024-03-25 (arXiv v2; accepted to International Journal of Computer Vision 25.03.2024)
claim: JEANIE costs about the same to compute as soft-DTW with 9-viewpoint test-time augmentation while scoring higher. On NTU-60 with a Titan RTX, per-query inference takes 0.020 s versus 0.019 s, and accuracy is 65.0% versus 56.8%. Generating the viewpoints was done once offline on CPU and is excluded from these times.
quote: soft-DTWaug 0.098 0.019 178.5 56.8 ... JEANIE 0.099 0.020 187.0 65.0 ... Among methods which use multiple viewpoints, JEANIE outperforms soft-DTWaug and TAPaug by 8.2% and 7.4% respectively. JEANIE outperforms ordinary soft-DTW and TAP by 11.3% and 10.8%.

published: 2024-03-25 (arXiv v2; accepted to International Journal of Computer Vision 25.03.2024)
claim: JEANIE needs 3D skeletons, because it simulates viewpoints by rotating hip-centred 3D joints with Euler angles or stereo projection. The authors report no JEANIE results on 2D keypoints, and on Kinetics-skeleton 3D input beats 2D by 3-4%. A monocular app using 2D BlazePose would need 3D lifting first.
quote: Note that we have no results on JEANIE or FVM for 2D coordinates as these require very different viewpoint modeling than 3D coordinates.

published: 2024-10-24 (arXiv v4; an earlier version appeared at CVPRW 2024)
claim: PnLCalib detects field keypoints and line extremities using HRNetV2-w48 heatmap networks. It computes an initial homography with RANSAC+DLT, recovers full camera intrinsics and extrinsics with Zhang's method, and then refines the camera pose by non-linear least squares over both points and lines (PnL). The pipeline is built around a 3D soccer field model, and the paper does not test other sports such as badminton.
quote: an optimization-based calibration pipeline that leverages a 3D soccer field model and a predefined set of keypoints

published: 2024-10-24 (arXiv v4; an earlier version appeared at CVPRW 2024)
claim: On the WorldCup 2014 test set, PnLCalib (single-view + PnL) reports IoU whole of 93.4% mean / 95.5% median, a mean projection error of 0.60 m and JaC5 of 85.2, against 59.4 JaC5 for the best prior method. On TS-WorldCup it reports IoU whole of 96.3% mean and a projection error of 0.23 m mean / 0.20 m median. These are reasonable reference accuracy levels for court-homography calibration, which affects shuttle speed accuracy in meters.
quote: This approach outperforms existing techniques in both multi-view and single-view 3D camera calibration tasks

published: 2024-10-24 (arXiv v4; an earlier version appeared at CVPRW 2024)
claim: The PnL point+line refinement raises the SoccerNet calibration Final Score by 2.8%. On SN22-test-center, FS goes from 74.4 to 78.7 and JaC5 from 75.8 to 80.6. This suggests that using line constraints alongside keypoints improves on keypoint-only homography.
quote: Additionally, our PnL refinement module showcases a 2.8% increase in the FS metric.

published: 2024-10-24 (arXiv v4; an earlier version appeared at CVPRW 2024)
claim: The method is far from real-time on mobile. On an RTX 2080 Ti GPU the plain multi-view model runs at about 7 Hz, falling to about 4 Hz with PnL refinement. For a Snapdragon 680 phone app, it fits one-time or per-session calibration (or cloud post-processing), not per-frame on-device inference.
quote: the inference speed decreases to an average of 4 Hz

published: 2024-10-24 (arXiv v4; an earlier version appeared at CVPRW 2024)
claim: Calibration needs at least four visible keypoints and fails under extreme lens distortion such as fisheye shots. A phone camera framing must therefore keep enough court-line intersections in view.
quote: a minimum of four keypoints are visible

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Science vol. 4(2), pp. 11-19; received 2021-11-29, accepted 2022-11-10)
claim: Compared against a 9-camera Vicon motion-capture reference at 500 Hz (a reflective marker on the shuttlecock), a Doppler radar gun (Stalker Sport, 250 Hz) underestimated badminton smash shuttlecock velocity by about 9.7% on average. A racket-handle IMU (Zepp Tennis) underestimated it by about 13.6%. By skill level, the radar deltas were -14.1%, -9.8% and -6.9% for novice, intermediate and expert. The sample was 34 players hitting a shuttle suspended from a string in the lab. Any radar 'ground truth' used to validate a vision-based speed estimate therefore carries a systematic low bias of roughly 7-14%.
quote: In terms of validity, radar and motion sensor provides an accurate measure but underestimate projectile velocity (-9.7% and -13.6% respectively).

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Science vol. 4(2), pp. 11-19; received 2021-11-29, accepted 2022-11-10)
claim: Radar velocity correlated strongly with the 500 Hz high-speed camera reference (r = 0.917, fitted line y = 0.9447x + 6.703). The handle-mounted IMU correlated only moderately (r = 0.682). Even so, the concurrent-validity CV against the camera was above the 10% adequacy threshold for both devices (about 12.5% for radar and 12.1% for the motion sensor). So the radar ranks shots well but does not match the camera's absolute values.
quote: the Pearson product moment correlation coefficient showed almost perfect correlation between the radar and the high-speed camera measurements for velocity (r= 0.917; p < 0.001); and good correlation between the motion sensor and the high-speed camera measurements (r=0.682; p < 0.001)

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Science vol. 4(2), pp. 11-19; received 2021-11-29, accepted 2022-11-10)
claim: The authors say a standard video camera at 50 fps measures shuttle velocity to only about +/-5 m/s. The gap between elite and highly skilled players is about 10 m/s, so they consider standard-frame-rate video inadequate for shuttlecock speed. They also put the accuracy of high-speed and 3D setups (120-500 fps) at 12-50 m/s depending on frame rate. This is cited background, not something measured in this study, but it applies directly to a 30-60 fps phone pipeline.
quote: The difference of velocity between elite and high skilled players is about 10 m.s-1 (Phomsoupha & Laffaye, 2014), whereas the velocity accuracy of a camera at 50 fps is about 5 m.s-1. This showed that it is impossible to assess a badminton shuttlecock velocity with such devices.

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Science vol. 4(2), pp. 11-19; received 2021-11-29, accepted 2022-11-10)
claim: Shuttlecock speed falls off logarithmically after racket contact, following V = -9.2 ln(T) + 2.4 (V in m/s, T in ms). Speed roughly halves within 0.05 s of leaving the racket. At 30 fps (33 ms per frame), estimating speed from pixel displacement between frames therefore misses the peak unless it is corrected with a drag-aware model.
quote: Phomsoupha & Laffaye (2014) showed that the shuttlecock velocity V (in m.s-1) is a logarithmic function of time T (in ms) as follow: V= -9.2 ln(T) +2.4, meaning that the velocity is divided by two times just 0.05 sec after the end of the racket contact.

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Science vol. 4(2), pp. 11-19; received 2021-11-29, accepted 2022-11-10)
claim: Test-retest reliability across two sessions was good for all three systems. Mean ICCs were 0.907 for the radar (range 0.88-0.94), 0.840 for the motion sensor (0.78-0.89) and 0.940 for the 500 Hz high-speed camera (0.92-0.96). The matching mean CVs were 5.8%, 7.7% and 4.3%. The authors add that radar placement and angle affect reproducibility, because a radar gun measures only radial velocity and always underestimates the true speed.
quote: The means of the ICCs was 0.907 ± 0.027 (range 0.88-0.94), 0.840 ± 0.054 (range 0.78-0.89) and 0.940 ± 0.018 (range 0.92-0.96) for the radar, the motion sensor and the high-speed cameras, respectively.

claim: RTMPose-m reaches 75.8% AP on COCO val2017 (with flip test) at 90+ FPS on an Intel i7-11700 CPU (ONNXRuntime) and 430+ FPS on a GTX 1660 Ti (TensorRT FP16). RTMPose-s reaches 72.2% AP at 70+ FPS on a Snapdragon 865. Caveat (not from the paper): the app's Snapdragon 680 target is a weaker chip than the 865, so expect lower FPS.
quote: Our RTMPose-m achieves 75.8% AP on COCO with 90+ FPS on an Intel i7-11700 CPU and 430+ FPS on an NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti GPU ... Our RTMPose-s model achieves 72.2% AP on COCO with 70+ FPS on a Snapdragon 865 chip, outperforming existing open-source libraries.

claim: On a 1,045-image COCO-SinglePerson subset of val2017 (no flip test), RTMPose is far more accurate than the app's current MediaPipe BlazePose and than MoveNet. Table 5: BlazePose-Lite 29.3 AP, BlazePose-Full 35.4 AP, MoveNet Lightning 53.6 AP, MoveNet Thunder 64.8 AP (both MoveNet scores use double inference), RTMPose-t 72.1 AP (0.67 GFLOPs including the RTMDet-nano detector), RTMPose-s 77.1 AP (0.91 GFLOPs), RTMPose-m 82.4 AP (2.23 GFLOPs).
quote: we construct a COCO-SinglePerson dataset that contains 1045 single-person images from the COCO val2017 set to evaluate RTMPose as well as other approaches ... The evaluation results in Table 5 show that RTMPose archives superior performance and efficiency even compared to previous solutions tailored for the single-person scenario.

claim: Measured mobile latency on a Snapdragon 865 (ncnn, 4 threads, 256x192 input), pose model only, FP32/FP16: RTMPose-t 15.84/9.02 ms (68.4 AP with ground-truth boxes), RTMPose-s 25.01/13.89 ms (72.8 AP), RTMPose-m 49.46/26.44 ms (77.3 AP), RTMPose-l 85.75/45.37 ms (78.3 AP). Full mobile pipeline with the RTMDet-nano detector (Table 12): 18.78 ms (t, 64.4 AP), 21.68 ms (s, 68.5 AP), 32.12 ms (m, 73.2 AP), 47.64 ms (l, 74.2 AP).
quote: We deploy RTMPose on the Snapdragon 865 chip with ncnn and inference with 4 threads.

claim: RTMPose's video inference pipeline borrows BlazePose's skip-frame detection, running the person detector only every K frames and taking boxes from the previous pose in between. It smooths keypoints over time with a One-Euro filter (after OKS-based pose NMS), a different approach from the app's current EMA smoothing.
quote: We use the skip-frame detection mechanism as in BlazePose [3], where human detection is performed every K frames ... to achieve smooth prediction over frames, we use OKS-based pose NMS and OneEuro [9] filter in the post-processing stage.

claim: RTMPose replaces heatmaps with a SimCC coordinate-classification head of two fully-connected layers, which makes it simple to deploy. In Table 1, the trimmed SimCC head uses 0.002 GFLOPs and 0.079M parameters, against 1.425 GFLOPs and 10.49M for a heatmap head, at 71.3 vs 71.8 AP. On whole-body pose (COCO-WholeBody V1.0, 133 keypoints including hands and feet), RTMPose-x reaches 65.3 AP.
quote: SimCC uses a very simple architecture of two fully-connected layers for prediction, making it easy to deploy on various backends.

claim: On AIST++ (dance) with VIBE poses, SmoothNet beats the One-Euro, Savitzky-Golay and Gaussian1d filters on both jitter and accuracy: Accel 4.15 and MPJPE 97.47 mm, against 31.64 / 106.90 for raw VIBE. The paper reports this as an 86.88% Accel reduction and an 8.82% MPJPE reduction. At comparable smoothness, One-Euro does much worse (Accel 4.67, MPJPE 135.71), and even when One-Euro is tuned for its lowest MPJPE it is less accurate and less smooth than SmoothNet (Accel 10.82, MPJPE 108.55).
quote: SmoothNet achieves the best performance, and it reduces Accel by 86.88% and MPJPE by 8.82% compared to the original pose estimation results... Among the three filters, the one-Euro filter shows inferior performance, and we attribute it to the real-time frame-by-frame jitter mitigation strategy used in it.

claim: SmoothNet is very small: about 0.33M parameters, with a default window of T=32 and step 1. The paper reports average inference above 1.3k fps on a CPU and 46.8k fps on an A100 GPU. That cost is small enough to sit on top of an on-device pose estimator or run in cloud post-processing.
quote: The input window size T is 32 and the moving step size s is 1... The parameters of SmoothNet is 0.33M, and the average inference time is less than 1.3k fps on a CPU and 46.8k on an A100-SXM4-40GB GPU.

claim: SmoothNet works on 2D keypoints as well as 3D, which matters for an app that runs a 2D estimator such as BlazePose. On Human3.6M it cut 2D Accel from 1.01 to 0.13 px/frame^2 for HRNet and from 2.91 to 0.14 for CPN, while MPJPE improved slightly (HRNet 4.59 to 4.54 px). On the worst 1% of frames, Accel fell by about 90% on average. The model was trained only on FCN 3D outputs, so these results also test transfer to other estimators.
quote: The Accel of all the backbones followed by our pose refinement method is significantly reduced, and MPJPE is also reduced to some extent... On average, the estimated Accel on these poses are decreased by about 90%.

claim: SmoothNet is not causal: each window uses future frames, so it can't refine poses in real time, frame by frame. This limits it to offline or cloud post-processing. A causal filter such as One-Euro or EMA would still be needed for live on-device feedback.
quote: SmoothNet is a sliding-window-based model, which limits its use in real-time systems since we can not aggregate future poses to refine the historical poses.

claim: Window size trades smoothness against accuracy. On VIBE-AIST++, Accel falls steadily from 17.89 at W=2 to 4.03 at W=256. MPJPE improves up to about 64-128 frames, while PA-MPJPE is best at W=32 (69.67), and all three metrics level off beyond 64 frames. The authors recommend W=64. The paper also finds that fixed low-pass filters trade jitter against lag and fail on long-term jitter, which shows up on rare or occluded poses (for example, fast smash motion would likely be affected).
quote: As the window size becomes longer, the Accel decreases consistently, but the MPJPE and PA-MPJPE initially decrease, then begin to increase slightly, indicating that when the size exceeds 64 frames, the results of the three metrics tend to be saturated. Therefore, 64 frames can be suitable to balance the smoothness and precision.

claim: FreeTrack (Yu et al., Machine Vision and Applications 37:167, 2026) reconstructs 3D shuttlecock trajectories from a single monocular camera far more accurately than MonoTrack. Validated by landing-point error on its own set of 96 sequences (about 17k frames, six stroke types), it cut error from 170.9 to 7.8 cm on Clears and from 30.5 to 5.7 cm on Net Drops. Smashes went from 103.5 to 8.9 cm, flat drives from 97.8 to 4.8, and serves from 86.0 to 8.7. Note that landing-point error is an indirect proxy, since no dense 3D badminton ground truth exists.
quote: reducing landing point errors by an order of magnitude in complex strokes (e.g., from 170 cm to 7.8 cm in Clear shots).

claim: FreeTrack fits no drag or kinematic model. It assumes each flight between two strikes lies in one vertical plane, anchors that plane at the striking frame and at the hitter's ground point (midpoint of the feet), and intersects each calibrated camera ray with the plane. Calibration is a six-point DLT from the four court corners and the two net-post tops, and it must be redone whenever the camera moves or zooms. This is a lightweight, physics-free option for stages 2 and 3 (3D trajectory and calibration).
quote: the trajectory is physically confined to a single vertical plane for the duration of its flight between two strikes

claim: FreeTrack's 3D reconstruction runs at 0.705 ms per frame, 83.14 times faster than MonoTrack's 46.815 ms per frame. Timing covered 9 badminton samples (3,291 frames) under the same timing scope. That speed makes per-frame 3D lifting plausible on a mobile device or in cheap cloud post-processing.
quote: Overall, FreeTrack is 83.14 times faster than MonoTrack under the same timing scope.

claim: For 2D shuttlecock detection, FreeTrack uses a fine-tuned YOLOv12 with TrackNet as a fallback. On 1,538 annotated broadcast frames it scored a mean distance error of 28.82 px and 0.846 accuracy within 5 px, the best against MonoTrack, Geetha et al. (2025), the original TrackNet (2019) and plain YOLOv12. The comparison did not include TrackNetV2 or V3, so it says little about TrackNetV3 or later.
quote: with the lowest mean distance error of 28.82 pixels and the highest accuracy of 0.846.

claim: A learned striking-frame detector beat MonoTrack and WASB (Where Is The Ball) on F1 at ±5, ±10 and ±15 frame tolerances. It is an XGBoost classifier on four kinematic features, with a second re-scoring pass and an alternating-hitter rule that recovers missed hits. The test set was small: 1,761 frames from five clips with 64 positive hits. This supports replacing wrist-velocity peak thresholding with a lightweight learned detector for stage 5. Exact F1 values sit in Table 4, which was not visible in the fetched text.
quote: Our FreeTrack achieves the best F1-score under all tolerance intervals

claim: For tracking the shuttlecock, the authors use an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) rather than a classic linear Kalman filter. They give the shuttlecock's nonlinear aerodynamics as the reason, because the classic filter requires linearization. This bears on replacing the app's constant-velocity Kalman filter. The filter's error statistics are only in Table I (an image), so the extracted text has no numbers comparing UKF and KF.
quote: we utilize the unscented Kalman filter (UKF) algorithm instead of the classic Kalman filter to filter the errors of measurement and recognition algorithm.

claim: The paper models air resistance on the shuttlecock as quadratic in velocity, and says drag coefficients differ notably between feather and synthetic shuttlecocks. This means a physics- or drag-aware trajectory model needs drag parameters set per shuttle type. A constant-velocity model ignores drag altogether.
quote: The air resistance force is proportional to the square of a shuttlecock velocity

claim: To predict the trajectory and landing point, the authors use three RBF neural networks, one per axis (X, Y, Z), that take velocity and elapsed time as input. This replaces a closed-form drag model. The networks were trained on more than 1500 manually collected stereo tracks, and 609 randomly selected tracks were used for testing.
quote: A trajectory data set containing more than 1500 tracks has been collected manually

claim: The RBF prediction model computes the shuttlecock's landing (drop-point) state in about 10 ms per prediction. That makes it fast enough for real-time use. The text gives no landing-point error in physical units (cm or mm); the error appears only in Figure 9.
quote: The experiment verifies that the prediction model can calculate the state of the drop point in 10 ms on average.

claim: The system depends on a special capture setup: two cameras (stereo, not one camera) with infrared filters and IR lights, a reflective marker stuck on the shuttlecock's cork, and detection by three-frame differencing. Its 3D tracking results therefore do not carry over directly to a single unmodified smartphone camera.
quote: the two infrared filters and two infrared lights are added in the front of the cameras

claim: On the full VideoBadminton dataset (18 stroke classes, 8:1:1 split), the RGB model SlowFast scored best of the seven models tested, with 82.80% Top-1, 97.54% Top-5 and 73.80% mean class accuracy.
quote: SlowFast (2019) | 82.80% | 97.54% | 73.80% (Table 3 row: Top1 Acc | Top5 Acc | Mean Cls Acc); the authors call SlowFast the "standout method"

claim: Among skeleton-based models on the full VideoBadminton dataset, PoseC3D reached 80.76% Top-1 (67.18% mean class accuracy), about 2 points behind SlowFast. ST-GCN reached only 74.41% Top-1 (61.44% mean class accuracy). This suggests that a heatmap-volume pose model is clearly better than a plain graph-convolution model for badminton stroke classification.

VideoBadminton has 18 fine-grained stroke categories in 7,822 clips (about 145 minutes) from 19 university players. It was recorded at 60 fps and 1280x960 by a fixed camera about 2 m behind the baseline. This makes it a benchmark more fine-grained than the app's 6-class scheme, and its camera setup is close to a phone placed behind the court.
quote: It incorporates 18 categories of badminton actions, with a total of 7,822 clips ... Operating at a frame rate of 60fps, the DFK 37AUX273 captured the fast-paced movements ... The camera was positioned approximately 2 meters behind the baseline of the badminton court

claim: With little data (10 or 50 clips per class), the skeleton model ST-GCN beat the RGB models. On VideoBadminton-50 it reached 60.70% Top-1 and led in every metric except Top-5, where PoseC3D scored slightly higher (89.87% vs 89.25%). Accuracy rose sharply with more samples per class. This suggests that pose-based models are more data-efficient for small custom datasets.
quote: ST-GCN "leads in all metrics" (VideoBadminton-50 subset discussion); "increasing the number of samples per class leads to significantly better model performance"

claim: The transformer video models did poorly on fine-grained badminton strokes. MViT-V2 collapsed to 14.23% Top-1 (10.76% mean class accuracy), and TimeSformer reached only 73.18% Top-1. This argues against assuming a generic video transformer will beat CNN or pose baselines in this domain.
quote: MViT-V2 (2022) | 14.23% | 62.23% | 10.76% (Table 3 row); MViT-V2 shows "notably lower scores across all metrics"

claim: On ShuttleSet (25 merged stroke classes; 36,492 strokes from 44 broadcast matches), BST-CG-AP reaches 0.8254 accuracy / 0.7983 macro-F1 with fixed-width clipping, ahead of TemPose-TF (0.8189/0.7943), ST-GCN (0.7758/0.7352), SkateFormer (0.7710/0.7363), ProtoGCN (0.7746/0.7306) and BlockGCN (0.7652/0.7298). With the paper's own clipping strategy it reaches 0.8322 / 0.8097, against 0.8235 / 0.8028 for TemPose-TF. These numbers come from Tables 1 and 2. The margin over TemPose is small (under 1 point) and was reported on fine-grained classes, not a 6-class taxonomy.
quote: Notably, our BST series achieves some improvement over TemPose on 18/20 metrics when using the fixed-width clipping strategy.

claim: BST is a multimodal model. It fuses 2D player pose (joints and bones), the shuttlecock's 2D trajectory and player court positions, using TCN, Transformer encoders and a Cross Transformer that relates pose and position to the shuttle trajectory. Its inputs come from RTMPose (via MMPose) for 2D pose and TrackNetV3 (attention version) for shuttle positions. MotionBERT 3D lifting was also run, but the models use the 2D poses.
quote: For the shuttlecock trajectories, we utilize the 2D shuttlecock positions generated by TrackNetV3 for each clip.

claim: On BadmintonDB (18 classes, 7,658 strokes from 8 singles matches), every model scores far lower. The best BST variant, BST-AP, reaches 0.6517 accuracy / 0.5799 macro-F1, against TemPose-TF at 0.6199/0.5448, ST-GCN at 0.5602/0.4870 and ProtoGCN at 0.5656/0.4798 (Table 4). BST-CG-AP, the best variant on ShuttleSet, is not the best here (0.6392/0.5580).
quote: contains 7658 strokes across 8 badminton singles matches after data cleaning.

claim: BST is a lightweight model, which suggests it could run on a phone. BST-CG-AP has 1.85M parameters, against 1.71M for TemPose-TF, 3.08M for ST-GCN, 4.11M for ProtoGCN, 2.38M for SkateFormer and 1.50M for BlockGCN (Table A). FLOPs and mobile latency are not reported.
quote: Model training speed per epoch on ShuttleSet and the numbers of their parameters.

claim: Stroke clips are cut around hit frames that are already annotated: a fixed-width window of half the FPS (0.5 s), with neighboring hits capped at 1.5 s. Sequence lengths are 30 or 100 frames on ShuttleSet and 72 on BadmintonDB. On TenniSet (6 classes) every method is close to saturation; BST-AP scores 0.9923 accuracy and ST-GCN 0.9890. The paper claims state-of-the-art results across all three datasets.
quote: Through experiments, we show that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods

claim: On ShuttleSet (40 cleaned matches, 33,429 strokes, 30/5/5 train/val/test match split, 31 stroke classes), TemPose-TF-ASF reaches 0.854 accuracy, 0.761 macro-F1 and 0.945 top-2 accuracy with 1.95M parameters. That beats the TemPose-TF baseline (0.835 / 0.742 / 0.927, 1.71M params) and BST-CG-AP (0.838 / 0.723 / 0.942, 1.88M params).
quote: Table 2: TemPose-TF-ASF | 1.95M | 0.854 | 0.761 | 0.945; TemPose-TF | 1.71M | 0.835 | 0.742 | 0.927; BST-CG-AP | 1.88M | 0.838 | 0.723 | 0.942. Abstract: "Experiments on a large-scale badminton match dataset show consistent improvements over the baseline and its variants in terms of Accuracy and Macro-F1."

claim: On the same ShuttleSet benchmark, the badminton-specific multimodal transformers (TemPose-TF, BST-CG-AP) beat general-purpose skeleton action models. BlockGCN reaches 0.793 Acc / 0.657 macro-F1 and SkateFormer 0.808 / 0.665, against 0.835 to 0.838 Acc and 0.723 to 0.742 macro-F1 for the badminton models. This suggests that generic GCN-style skeleton models underperform pose+shuttle+court fusion models for fine-grained stroke classification.
quote: Section 4.2: "comparisons with several state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, including BlockGCN, SkateFormer, and BST-CG-AP, were conducted." Table 2: BlockGCN | 1.69M | 0.793 | 0.657 | 0.906; SkateFormer | 2.38M | 0.808 | 0.665 | 0.897

claim: The best stroke classifiers here fuse several inputs: skeleton joints and bones of both players, player court positions, and shuttlecock trajectories. The trajectories come from TrackNetV3 and the court lines from MonoTrack or TennisCourtDetector. In practice this ties the stroke-classification stage to the detection and court-calibration stages upstream.
quote: "shuttlecock trajectories are extracted using TrackNetV3"; "Court lines are extracted using either the method proposed in MonoTrack" "or a deep learning-based approach, TennisCourtDetector"

claim: The Adjacent-Stroke Fusion (ASF) module adds context from the stroke types predicted for the preceding and following strokes. It is plug-in: it improved every model it was added to, raising TemPose-V macro-F1 from 0.658 to 0.701 and BlockGCN from 0.657 to 0.673. It needs two-stage inference, where the baseline's first-pass predictions serve as context. Because it uses future strokes, it is suited to post-rally or offline (cloud) processing rather than strictly causal real-time use.
quote: "Preliminary predictions from the baseline model are reused as estimated temporal context." "All augmented models consistently outperform their original versions." Table 2: TemPose-V | 0.798 | 0.658 vs TemPose-V-ASF | 0.814 | 0.701

claim: All results use a fine-grained label set of 31 stroke categories, re-derived from ShuttleSet's original 19 (which include a 'none' class), and ShuttleSet is the only dataset evaluated. The numbers do not carry over directly to a 6-class (smash/drop/clear/net/serve/defensive) setup or to the VideoBadminton and BadmintonDB datasets. The paper reports parameter counts only, with no latency figures.
quote: "After these adjustments, the final classification setup consists of 31 stroke categories." "The original ShuttleSet contains 19 distinct stroke categories, including a 'none' class."

claim: On RacketVision's badminton split (pro broadcast footage at 1080p, metrics computed at 1920x1080), TrackNetV3 trained on all three sports with a background-median input and 4 frames is the best shuttle tracker. It reaches mAP@50 83.1, recall 0.865 and mean distance error (MDE) 1.54 px. The best single-sport TrackNetV3 (background median, 4 frames) reaches mAP 72.5 and MDE 2.07 px. Multi-sport training therefore adds 14.6% mAP on badminton.
quote: the MS model boosts mAP by a significant 19.2% in Tennis (81.9 vs. 68.7) and 14.6% in Badminton (83.1 vs. 72.5).

claim: A generic single-frame YOLO11 detector does much worse than heatmap trackers on the badminton shuttle. From Table 3: YOLO11 gets recall 0.548 and MDE 29.3 px (mAP 72.1). WASB gets recall 0.803 and MDE 4.03 px. TrackNetV3 with background median and 4 frames gets recall 0.865 and MDE 2.07 px. RTMDet gets recall 0.721 and MDE 38.2 px. So the YOLO-family detector's mAP is comparable, but it misses about 45% of visible shuttles and localizes them about 14x worse.

Adding a static background-median frame as an extra input to TrackNetV3 (single frame) cuts the shuttle localization error (MDE) on badminton by 54.8%, from 7.39 px to 3.34 px. It also raises badminton mAP from 57.8 to 67.7.
quote: background modeling reduces MDE by a remarkable 54.0% for Table Tennis, 61.4% for Tennis, and 54.8% for Badminton.

claim: For predicting future ball trajectories from past positions, naively concatenating racket-pose features does worse than a ball-only model: badminton short-horizon LSTM ADE rises from 37.5 to 45.7. Cross-attention fusion (ball as query, racket as key/value) is best but only slightly better: badminton short ADE goes from 37.5 to 37.0, and long-horizon LSTM ADE/FDE goes from 118.7/194.7 to 114.6/187.6. Across all settings, the LSTM backbone beats a 4-layer Transformer.
quote: In Short Badminton, ADE improves from 37.5 to 37.0.

claim: A top-down RTMPose model (RTMDet as the detector) trained on all three sports estimates 5 badminton racket keypoints at PCK@0.2 88.5, MPJPE 5.00 px and mOKS 0.668. The side keypoints (left/right) are much less accurate (74.6/75.5%) than top/bottom/handle (above 97%).
quote: badminton excels in pose quality metrics with the lowest MPJPE (5.00px) and highest mOKS (0.668), demonstrating the effectiveness of cross-sport knowledge transfer.

claim: On the test split of the Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset, TrackNetV3 gets 97.51% accuracy, 97.79% precision, 99.33% recall and 98.56% F1 at 25.11 FPS. TrackNetV2 gets 94.98% accuracy and 97.03% F1 at 27.70 FPS. So V3 raises F1 by about 1.5 points and recall by about 4.8 points, at a small cost in speed and precision.
quote: TrackNetV2 | 94.98% | 99.64% | 94.56% | 97.03% | 27.70 ... TrackNetV3 | 97.51% | 97.79% | 99.33% | 98.56% | 25.11 ("Performance on the test split of Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset")

claim: A general-purpose YOLO detector (YOLOv7) does much worse than heatmap-based TrackNet models at shuttlecock detection on the same test split: 57.82% accuracy and 68.00% F1. It is the fastest model in the table at 34.77 FPS. This suggests generic YOLO detectors, such as the app's current YOLOv8n, are poorly suited to the tiny, fast shuttlecock compared with TrackNet-style models.

TrackNetV3 has two modules. The first is a trajectory-prediction (tracking) network that takes an estimated background image as extra input and is trained with mixup augmentation. The second is a rectification module (InpaintNet) that builds repair masks from the predicted trajectory and fills in occluded or missed points by inpainting.
quote: We present TrackNetV3, a model composed of two core modules: trajectory prediction and rectification. The trajectory prediction module leverages an estimated background as auxiliary data to locate the shuttlecock in spite of the fluctuating visual interferences. This module also incorporates mixup data augmentation ... we create repair masks by analyzing the predicted trajectory, subsequently rectifying the path via inpainting.

claim: TrackNetV3 needs a background image computed as the median frame over a match or rally, and it works on multi-frame windows: an 8-frame sequence for the tracking network and a 16-frame sequence for the rectification module. This makes it a natural fit for offline or cloud post-processing rather than strict per-frame on-device streaming.
quote: If available, the dataset will use the median image of the match; otherwise, it will use the median image of the rally. ... python train.py --model_name TrackNet --seq_len 8 --epochs 30 --batch_size 10 --bg_mode concat --alpha 0.5

claim: The official TrackNetV3 code and pretrained checkpoints (TrackNet_best.pt and InpaintNet_best.pt) are public. The README states MIT licensing, and the published FPS figures come from a PyTorch 1.10 desktop environment, not from mobile hardware.
quote: Develop Environment: Ubuntu 16.04.7 LTS, Python 3.8.7, torch 1.10.0 ... python predict.py --video_file test.mp4 --tracknet_file ckpts/TrackNet_best.pt --inpaintnet_file ckpts/InpaintNet_best.pt --save_dir prediction

The method uses frame-difference motion prompts plus R(2+1)D spatiotemporal blocks, so it needs multi-frame input, unlike single-frame YOLO detectors.
quote: We evaluate TrackNetV5 on the public badminton dataset [5, 6] with frames resized to 512 × 288. The value of T (e.g., sequence length) is set to 5. A prediction is considered a True Positive (TP) if the distance to the ground truth is within 4 pixels [5].
