claim: The authors argue that single-frame YOLO-family detectors, including YOLOv12, are ill-suited to shuttlecock tracking for two reasons: backbone downsampling loses features of tiny objects, and without temporal context a detector cannot separate a motion-blurred shuttle (up to 426 km/h) from background noise. This is a qualitative argument with no YOLO baseline numbers in the paper.
quote: The aggressive downsampling in these backbones often leads to the loss of fine-grained features for minuscule objects. Furthermore, the lack of temporal context makes it nearly impossible for static detectors to distinguish a blurred shuttlecock (i.e., traveling at speeds up to 426 km/h) from complex background noise.

claim: On the TrackNetV2 Badminton (shuttlecock) dataset, with a 4-pixel distance threshold, WASB with oversampling (Step=1, 1.5M params) reaches F1 93.1 / Accuracy 89.0 / AP 91.6 at 34.3 FPS. The authors' re-implementations score lower: TrackNetV2 (11.3M params) gets F1 90.5 / Acc 85.6 / AP 83.6 at 77.0 FPS, and MonoTrack (2.9M) gets F1 90.9 / Acc 85.9 / AP 84.9 at 75.5 FPS. FPS was measured on a V100 GPU.
quote: TrackNetV2 [75] 11.3M ... 90.5 85.6 83.6 77.0 ... MonoTrack [50] 2.9M ... 90.9 85.9 84.9 75.5 ... WASB (Ours, Step=1) 1.5M ... 93.1 89.0 91.6 34.3 [Badminton columns: F1, Acc., AP, FPS]; 'We set the distance threshold τ = 4 [pixel] to compute F1, Accuracy (Acc.) and Average Precision (AP)'

claim: Without oversampling (Step=3), WASB scores F1 91.6 / Acc 87.0 / AP 88.5 on Badminton at 70.4 FPS. That is close to TrackNetV2's speed with about 7.5x fewer parameters (1.5M vs 11.3M). Oversampling (Step=1) adds about +1.5 F1 and +3.1 AP but roughly halves throughput. Across datasets, WASB's best AP beats the best prior method by 7.8 to 16.8 points.
quote: WASB (Ours, Step=3) 1.5M ... 91.6 87.0 88.5 70.4 [Badminton]; 'with respect to AP, our best models significantly outperform the best existing methods by 7.8 ~16.8 %. Notice that WASB is not the fastest among the methods.'

claim: WASB works as follows. A small HRNet backbone, with strides removed from the stem, keeps high-resolution features instead of using a U-Net encoder-decoder. It takes 3 consecutive frames resized to 288x512 and outputs one heatmap per frame (multiple-in multiple-out). It is trained with real-valued Gaussian ground-truth maps and quality focal loss, applied only to hard-to-localize samples. At inference the ball position is taken as the center of the heatmap values. All timings come from a V100 server GPU, not from a mobile device.
quote: N (cf. §3.1) is set to 3 and each image is resized to 288 × 512 to be fed into our model... We performed all the following experiments on an Ubuntu server with 4 V100 GPUs.

claim: The authors report that classical Kalman or particle filtering gave no improvement over their simple online candidate filtering, which uses a constant-acceleration local motion model. In the ablation, the online-tracking step itself added nothing on the Badminton dataset (F1 91.6 / AP 88.5 both with and without it). This bears on the app's current constant-velocity Kalman filter.
quote: we do not use filtering algorithms such as Kalman filter [...] and particle filter [...], since any performance improvement was not observed with them... online tracking does not contribute on the Soccer and Badminton datasets

claim: WASB predicts at most one ball (x, y) per frame. It was validated only on HD/FHD video at 25-30 fps, so performance at the app's 60 fps or on low-resolution phone input is untested. On the 1280x720, 30 fps Badminton dataset, the shuttle moves about 12 px per frame on average.
quote: While there are no theoretical limitations with respect to frame resolution and frame rate, our validation is limited to standard frame resolutions (e.g., HD, FHD) and frame rates (e.g., 25-30 FPS).

claim: On the shuttlecock (TrackNetV2/V3 badminton) benchmark, adding TrackNetV4's motion attention to TrackNetV3 raised accuracy from 95.7 to 96.4, precision went from 99.7 to 99.5, recall from 95.4 to 96.3 and F1 from 97.5 to 97.9. This TrackNetV3 (+Motion), i.e. TrackNetV4, configuration had the highest shuttlecock score in the paper's Table I (evaluated on 10,836 frames for the V3 protocol).
quote: Experimental results on the tennis ball and shuttlecock datasets show that our method enhances the tracking performance of both TrackNetV2 and V3 ... our motion-aware fusion mechanism still achieves improvements of over 0.8%

claim: A generic box detector does much worse than heatmap TrackNet models on shuttlecock detection. On the same shuttlecock dataset, YOLOv7 scored Acc 57.8 / Prec 78.5 / Rec 60.0 / F1 68.0, against TrackNetV2 at Acc 85.6 / F1 90.6 and TrackNetV3 at Acc 95.7 / F1 97.5. This suggests the app's YOLOv8n shuttle detector is the weak link compared with a TrackNet-family heatmap model.

The motion-attention module is a lightweight plug-in that costs very little speed. On the shuttlecock data, TrackNetV2 runs at 163.3 FPS and TrackNetV2 (+Motion) at 161.1 FPS, while accuracy improves from 85.6 to 86.6 and F1 from 90.6 to 91.4. TrackNetV3's reported 15.1 FPS covers the whole script, including data loading and file I/O, so it cannot be compared directly. Benchmark hardware was a desktop GPU, not mobile.
quote: a lightweight, plug-and-play extension of TrackNet ... TrackNetV4

claim: TrackNetV4's mechanism is frame-differencing maps, modulated by a learnable motion prompt layer, fused with high-level visual features. It targets the cases where TrackNetV1-V3 fail: partial occlusion and low visibility of small, fast, motion-blurred objects.
quote: fusing high-level visual features with learnable motion attention maps through a motion-aware fusion mechanism

claim: On the authors' own multi-ball dataset (3,279 evaluation frames), TrackNetV4 (v2) trained from scratch reached Acc 94.7 / F1 97.2 at 169.1 FPS, against TrackNetV2 at Acc 93.4 / F1 96.5 at 186.4 FPS. The v1 variant underperformed the baseline (Acc 91.8 / F1 95.7). Gains depend on the variant and on the fine-tuning learning rate.
quote: outperforms the baseline, with improvements of 1.3%, 1.2%, 0.3%, and 0.7% in accuracy

claim: UMEG-Net is a 2.2M-parameter graph model. Each frame's graph joins player skeletons, ball/shuttle keypoints and court-corner keypoints, and frames are linked by a parameter-free multi-scale temporal shift. In few-shot precise event spotting it beats the best baselines (E2E-Spot, T-DEED, F3ED, BlockGCN) by 1.3% to 5.5% F1evt and 1.3% to 16.4% Edit. On ShuttleSet in the 100-clip setting it scores 49.2 F1evt / 64.0 Edit, against 42.7/54.6 for E2E-Spot and 47.1/59.4 for BlockGCN.
quote: UMEG-Net consistently outperforms baseline methods, improving F1 scores by 1.3% to 5.5% and edit scores by 1.3% to 16.4%

claim: UMEG-Distill transfers knowledge from the frozen pose+shuttle+court graph teacher to an RGB student (VideoMAEv2 plus a bidirectional GRU) using unlabeled clips. It adds an average of 5.8% F1 and 6.7% Edit over UMEG-Net. On ShuttleSet (100-clip few-shot) it reaches 59.1 F1evt / 69.0 Edit, but the distilled model is about 67.8M parameters.
quote: Compared to UMEG-Net, it improves on average 5.8% in F1

claim: ShuttleSet works as a learned hit-frame benchmark: every shot is labeled with its exact racket-shuttle contact frame and one of 36 event types. The paper scores against a strict tolerance of 1 frame.
quote: Each shot is annotated with the exact racket–shuttle contact frame and its event type (36 categories).

claim: With full supervision, UMEG-Net roughly matches the RGB end-to-end E2E-Spot on ShuttleSet (71.4 vs 71.2 F1evt, both 76.1 Edit). It has the higher F1evt on 3 of 5 datasets (F3Set-Tennis, ShuttleSet, Figure Skating) and the lower on FineGym-BB and SoccerNet-BAS.
quote: It shows better performance in 3 out of 5 datasets.

claim: UMEG-Net gets its inputs from upstream detectors: top-down HRNet for 2D pose, a fine-tuned YOLOv8 for players and balls, TrackNetV3 for shuttle tracking on ShuttleSet, and deployed court-detection models for the four court corners. Its graph network is the smallest of all compared baselines at 2.2M parameters. The paper reports no inference latency.
quote: with the fewest parameters (2.2M) among all baselines.

claim: Fusing TrackNet shuttle trajectories with a YOLOv7 player-swing (hit-action) detector through a rule-based Shot Refinement Algorithm (SRA) raises hit/shot-extraction precision from 0.588 to 0.897 and F1 from 0.723 to 0.905, while recall drops slightly from 0.936 to 0.913. Shots are matched at temporal IoU of 0.5 on BWF broadcast match videos. The abstract calls the precision figure 'accuracy'.
quote: Our proposed method achieves an accuracy of 89.7%, a recall rate of 91.3%, and an F1 rate of 90.5% ... compared to the use of TrackNet alone, which yields 58.8% accuracy, 93.6% recall, and 72.3% F1 score.

claim: Hit-frame detection based only on the shuttle trajectory (TrackNet direction changes) has high recall but many false positives, with precision of 0.588. Adding a learned visual swing detector (YOLOv7 trained on manually labelled player hit actions) is what removes most of those false hits. This argues against relying on a single kinematic cue such as wrist-velocity peaks or trajectory inflection alone.
quote: the trajectory-based method only yielded a precision of 0.588, a recall rate of 0.936, and an F1 score of 0.723

claim: Shot-type classification uses an XGBoost classifier over 7 classes (clear, drive, smash, net, drop, lift, push). Its accuracy is 72.1%, 65.4% and 54.1% at t-IoU thresholds of 0.5, 0.85 and 0.95 when the SRA-refined segments are used, compared with 71.9%, 61.0% and 38.8% from TrackNet-only segmentation. Table 2 orders thresholds against values in reverse of the abstract's wording. Better hit segmentation therefore improves the downstream stroke classifier most at strict temporal thresholds.
quote: the accuracy of shot type classification at three different thresholds is 72.1%, 65.4%, and 54.1%.

claim: The SRA refinement step adds about 0.14 s of processing per sample (0.032 s for TrackNet alone vs 0.174-0.175 s with SRA in Table 1). Both the shuttle tracker and the action detector produce false alarms and misses, especially when the player occludes the shuttle. The paper does not state which TrackNet version it uses or report FPS.
quote: Notably, both the shuttlecock-tracking and action-detection modules are susceptible to false alarms or detection misses.

claim: The evaluation uses Badminton World Federation (BWF) broadcast match videos: 69 matches and 1,582 rallies according to the abstract. The body reports different subset counts (e.g., 32 matches / 602 rallies / 8,975 images), so the dataset size is internally inconsistent. All footage is fixed broadcast-view, not smartphone capture.
quote: in 69 matches, with 1582 rallies of the Badminton World Federation (BWF) match videos

published: 2022-04-04 (v1; v2 revised 2022-05-18; CVSports workshop at CVPR 2022)
claim: MonoTrack's learned hit detector (HitNet, about 16K parameters, using shuttle, pose and court features) plus a sequence optimization step reaches F1 0.946 (94.3% recall, 94.9% precision). A derivative-based hit detector, which works much like the app's current velocity-peak thresholding, gets F1 0.699 on the same test set. HitNet without the optimization step reaches F1 0.866.
quote: Table 1: 'Derivative-based | 65.7% | 53.8% | 74.7% | 0.699' ... 'HitNet (All) | 78.1% | 76.4% | 97.2% | 0.866' ... 'HitNet+optimization | 94.3% | 89.7% | 94.9% | 0.946'; text: 'The network is compact in size (around 16K parameters) and can reach 86.3% accuracy.'

published: 2022-04-04 (v1; v2 revised 2022-05-18; CVSports workshop at CVPR 2022)
claim: MonoTrack reconstructs 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular video by modeling the shuttle as a particle under quadratic air drag, with a drag coefficient that can change per shot, plus court and shot-placement priors. On 10k synthetic trajectories the priors cut the average 3D error from 14.9 cm to 8.0 cm. Real matches have no 3D ground truth, so only 2D reprojection error was measured: 8.1-9.8 px bootstrapped and up to 37.1 px end-to-end (about 5% of image resolution).
quote: On average, adding the priors improves the error from 14.9 cm to 8.0 cm. ... The highest error is 37.1 pixels, or about 5% given the image resolution we are working with.

published: 2022-04-04 (v1; v2 revised 2022-05-18; CVSports workshop at CVPR 2022)
claim: MonoTrack's modified TrackNetV2 shuttle tracker raises tracking accuracy from 84.0% to 88.6% while shrinking the model from 11.3M to 2.9M parameters. Input is 288x512 and the model predicts three frames at once. No precision, recall or F1 is reported for this tracker.
quote: 88.6% accuracy from 84.0% in the original ... 2.9M parameters in our model versus 11.3M parameters

published: 2022-04-04 (v1; v2 revised 2022-05-18; CVSports workshop at CVPR 2022)
claim: MonoTrack's court detector raises the court detection success rate (IoU > 0.8) from 73.9% to 85.5%, with average IoU 0.97 vs 0.96. It also cuts detection time by about 40x. This supports homography-based court calibration as the basis for speed estimation.
quote: our proposed approach increases the success rate of court detection from 73.9% to 85.5%

published: 2022-04-04 (v1; v2 revised 2022-05-18; CVSports workshop at CVPR 2022)
claim: MonoTrack is trained and evaluated on 77k annotated frames from 26 international singles matches, with a test set of about 12k frames from 3 matches. Court detection was also tested on 40 more YouTube matches. All of this is broadcast-style footage, not smartphone video.
quote: In total, this dataset contains 77k annotated frames from 26 unique singles matches from international play.

claim: On the test split of the Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset, TrackNetV3 reaches 97.51% accuracy, 97.79% precision, 99.33% recall and 98.56% F1. TrackNetV2 reaches 94.98% accuracy, 99.64% precision, 94.56% recall and 97.03% F1. So V3 gains about 2.5 points of accuracy and about 1.5 points of F1, mostly through recall, while precision drops slightly.

A general-purpose YOLO detector (YOLOv7) does much worse than heatmap-based TrackNet models on the same shuttlecock test set: 57.82% accuracy, 59.96% recall and 68.00% F1. This suggests generic box detectors miss many shuttlecock frames.

TrackNetV3 is slightly slower than TrackNetV2: 25.11 FPS against 27.70 FPS. YOLOv7 is the fastest at 34.77 FPS. The README does not say what hardware these speeds were measured on, so they cannot be carried over to a Snapdragon 680 phone.

TrackNetV3 has two modules. A trajectory prediction module uses an estimated background (the median image of the match, or of the rally) as extra input, plus mixup augmentation. A separate rectification module (InpaintNet) builds repair masks from the predicted trajectory and fills in missing or incorrect positions by inpainting. The training commands use 8-frame sequences for tracking and 16-frame sequences for rectification.
quote: The trajectory prediction module leverages an estimated background as auxiliary data to locate the shuttlecock ... we create repair masks by analyzing the predicted trajectory ... If available, the dataset will use the median image of the match; otherwise, it will use the median image of the rally.

claim: The code and the pretrained checkpoints (TrackNet_best.pt and InpaintNet_best.pt) are released under the MIT License, so they can be used commercially or adapted for a mobile app.
quote: released under the MIT License

claim: A custom-trained YOLOv5 shuttlecock detector, trained on a self-annotated dataset of 15,000 images all taken from a perpendicular side-on viewpoint, reached 93% precision, 87% recall and 91% mAP@0.5. No F1 score was given, and there was no comparison to TrackNet or other heatmap trackers.
quote: a precision of 93%, a recall of 87%, and a mean Average Precision at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (mAP@0.5) of 91%

claim: Against a Bushnell Speedster III radar gun over 20 smashes from one skilled player, filmed on an iPhone 16 at 30 fps, the vision system's peak smash speed had an MAE of 66.41 km/h and an RMSE of 74.68 km/h. It consistently read higher than the radar. The author blames the radar for missing the early, fastest phase of flight. Agreement 'at net' is described only in words, with no number.
quote: The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between the two methods for peak speed was 66.41 km/h ... the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) was 74.68 km/h.

claim: Court calibration uses no homography or 3D reconstruction. The user clicks two points on a court line to set one meters-per-pixel scale. The method assumes the camera is perpendicular to the plane of motion and cannot capture motion toward or away from the camera, which is the same family of limits as Ayto's current pixels-per-meter approach.
quote: Any movement along the z-axis (towards or away from the camera) is not captured

claim: Tracking uses a linear constant-velocity Kalman filter, SORT-style. The best candidate box is chosen with a composite score weighted 0.7 on Kalman prediction and 0.3 on YOLO confidence. Detections implying speeds below 5 km/h or above 375 km/h are thrown out, and detection runs at a low 0.1 confidence threshold to maximize recall.
quote: S_comp = (0.3·C_YOLO) + (0.7·P_Kalman). The weights are set empirically to prioritize temporal smoothness over raw detection confidence.

claim: The system ships as iOS (Swift) and Android (React Native) apps, but the paper reports no on-device inference latency or FPS. It treats TrackNetV2 only as an unsuitable broadcast-view dataset and leaves training on it to future work.
quote: train similar models on badminton-specific datasets like TrackNetV2

claim: On the COCO-SinglePerson val subset (1045 single-person images), top-down RTMPose with an RTMDet-nano detector reaches 72.1 AP (t), 77.1 AP (s), 82.4 AP (m) and 83.5 AP (l). MediaPipe BlazePose-Lite scores 29.3 AP, BlazePose-Full 35.4 AP, MoveNet Lightning 53.6 AP and MoveNet Thunder 64.8 AP (MoveNet with double inference). So RTMPose-t is about 37 AP higher than BlazePose-Full, the model the app uses now.
quote: The evaluation results in Table 5 show that RTMPose archives superior performance and efficiency even compared to previous solutions tailored for the single-person scenario. [Table 5: BlazePose-Lite 29.3; BlazePose-Full 35.4; MoveNet Lightning 53.6*; Thunder 64.8*; RTMPose-t 72.1; RTMPose-s 77.1; RTMPose-m 82.4; RTMPose-l 83.5]

claim: In the paper's mobile test (ncnn, 4 threads, Snapdragon 865), pose-model latency at 256x192 input is 9.02 ms for RTMPose-t (FP16, 15.84 ms FP32), 13.89 ms for RTMPose-s (FP16, 25.01 ms FP32), 26.44 ms for RTMPose-m (FP16, 49.46 ms FP32) and 45.37 ms for RTMPose-l (FP16, 85.75 ms FP32). These figures are for a Snapdragon 865, a flagship chip faster than the Snapdragon 680 the app targets.
quote: We deploy RTMPose on the Snapdragon 865 chip with ncnn and inference with 4 threads. [Table 10: RTMPose-t 0.36 GFLOPs, AP(GT) 68.4, FP32 15.84 ms, FP16 9.02 ms; RTMPose-s 72.8, 25.01, 13.89; RTMPose-m 77.3, 49.46, 26.44; RTMPose-l 78.3, 85.75, 45.37]

claim: On full COCO val2017, RTMPose-m reaches 75.8% AP at over 90 FPS on an Intel i7-11700 CPU and over 430 FPS on a GTX 1660 Ti. RTMPose-s reaches 72.2% AP at over 70 FPS on a Snapdragon 865. RTMPose-x reaches 65.3% AP on COCO-WholeBody.
quote: Our RTMPose-m achieves 75.8% AP on COCO with 90+ FPS on an Intel i7-11700 CPU and 430+ FPS on an NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti GPU, and RTMPose-x achieves 65.3% AP on COCO-WholeBody. ... Our RTMPose-s model achieves 72.2% AP on COCO with 70+ FPS on a Snapdragon 865 chip

claim: The RTMPose inference pipeline uses BlazePose-style skip-frame detection: the person detector runs only every K frames, and the boxes in between come from the previous pose. Temporal smoothing uses OKS-based pose NMS plus a One-Euro filter, not EMA.
quote: We use the skip-frame detection mechanism as in BlazePose [3], where human detection is performed every K frames, and in the interval frames the bounding boxes are generated from the last pose estimation results. Additionally, to achieve smooth prediction over frames, we use OKS-based pose NMS and OneEuro [9] filter in the post-processing stage.

claim: RTMPose locates keypoints with SimCC coordinate classification (separate x-axis and y-axis bin classifiers) on a CSPNeXt backbone instead of heatmaps. With the upsampling layers removed, the head needs 0.002 GFLOPs versus 1.425 GFLOPs for a heatmap head, at comparable AP (71.3 vs 71.8).
quote: RTMPose predicts keypoints using a SimCC-based [35] algorithm that treats keypoint localization as a classification task. Compared with heatmap-based algorithms [24, 59, 61, 65], the SimCC-based algorithm achieves competitive accuracy with lower computational effort.

claim: On AIST++ dance video (60 fps, fast complex motion) with VIBE as the pose estimator, SmoothNet cut acceleration error (jitter) from 31.64 to 4.15 mm/frame^2, an 86.88% reduction. It also cut MPJPE from 106.90 to 97.47 mm, an 8.82% reduction. This beat the best-tuned One-Euro, Savitzky-Golay and Gaussian1d filters on both metrics.
quote: SmoothNet achieves the best performance, and it reduces Accel by 86.88% and MPJPE by 8.82% compared to the original pose estimation results.

claim: In Table 1 on AIST++, the One-Euro filter was tuned to match SmoothNet's smoothness (Accel 4.67 vs 4.15). At that setting its MPJPE rose to 135.71 mm, versus 97.47 mm for SmoothNet and 105.71 mm for Gaussian1d. The authors call One-Euro the weakest of the three filters and blame its causal, frame-by-frame design.
quote: Among the three filters, the one-Euro filter shows inferior performance, and we attribute it to the real-time frame-by-frame jitter mitigation strategy used in it.

claim: SmoothNet is very light: 0.33M parameters, a default input window of T=32 frames with step 1, and inference above 1.3k fps on a CPU (46.8k fps on an A100). Window-size ablation: Accel drops steadily as the window grows, and results saturate past 64 frames, which the authors recommend as the best balance.
quote: The parameters of SmoothNet is 0.33M, and the average inference time is less than 1.3k fps on a CPU and 46.8k on an A100-SXM4-40GB GPU.

claim: SmoothNet works on a sliding window and needs future frames, so the authors say it is limited in real-time systems. For a live on-device feedback loop it either adds about a window's worth of latency or belongs in offline/cloud post-processing. A causal filter such as One-Euro is the alternative.
quote: SmoothNet is a sliding-window-based model, which limits its use in real-time systems since we can not aggregate future poses to refine the historical poses.

claim: SmoothNet is plug-and-play for 2D keypoint estimators, not just 3D. On Human3.6M 2D pose it cut HRNet's Accel from 1.01 to 0.13 px/frame^2 (MPJPE 4.59 to 4.54 px) and CPN's Accel from 2.91 to 0.14 (MPJPE 6.67 to 6.45 px). On the worst 1% of poses, Accel fell by about 90% on average.
quote: On average, the estimated Accel on these poses are decreased by about 90%.

claim: Zhi et al. (UESTC, Robotica 40(6), 2022) filter noisy 3D shuttlecock tracks with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) in place of a classic linear Kalman filter. Their reason is that drag is nonlinear: air resistance scales with the square of velocity, which a constant-velocity Kalman filter cannot capture. The UKF parameters were alpha=0.01, kappa=0, beta=2, and it was tested on 609 randomly chosen tracks. Per-track RMSE appears only in a table image; the page text gives no numbers.
quote: we utilize the unscented Kalman filter (UKF) algorithm instead of the classic Kalman filter ... The air resistance force is proportional to the square of a shuttlecock velocity

claim: The trajectory data came from a stereo (binocular) infrared camera rig, not a single camera. Shuttles were detected with a three-frame difference algorithm. More than 1500 tracks were collected by hand. This means the 3D tracking result does not carry over directly to a single-phone RGB setup.
quote: First, we have established a shuttlecock track data set by an infrared-based binocular vision system. ... A trajectory data set containing more than 1500 tracks has been collected manually

claim: Landing points are predicted by a radial basis function (RBF) neural network model rather than by integrating an explicit physics model. There are three RBF networks, each taking speed and time interval as its two inputs. Each network was trained on more than 2 million samples.
quote: Third, the radial basis function (RBF)-based track prediction model is designed.

claim: The RBF model computes the landing-point state in 10 ms on average. This was measured on a desktop CPU (Ryzen 5 2600X) with the model re-implemented in C++. The paper does not test on a phone.
quote: The experiment verifies that the prediction model can calculate the state of the drop point in 10 ms on average.

claim: The paper says it predicts trajectories in real time with high accuracy, but the page text gives no position error in cm or mm. Prediction error appears only in Figure 9, and there is no numeric comparison against a classic Kalman filter or any other baseline.
quote: the proposed method can predict the shuttlecock trajectory in real time at high accuracy

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Sci. 4(2):11-19; accepted 2022-11-10; journal web page dated 2025-03-22)
claim: In a 34-player smash study (12 novices, 11 intermediates, 11 experts), a Doppler radar gun (Stalker Sport, 250 Hz) underestimated peak shuttlecock velocity by an average of 9.7% against a 500 Hz, 9-camera Vicon reference. A racket-mounted IMU (Zepp Tennis) underestimated it by 13.6%. By skill level, radar bias was -14.1% for novices, -9.8% for intermediates and -6.9% for experts. So radar is a biased ground truth, not an exact one, for checking a camera-based speed estimator.
quote: In terms of validity, radar and motion sensor provides an accurate measure but underestimate projectile velocity (-9.7% and -13.6% respectively).

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Sci. 4(2):11-19; accepted 2022-11-10; journal web page dated 2025-03-22)
claim: The authors say a standard camera at 50 fps measures shuttle velocity only to within about 5 m/s, while elite and high-skilled players differ by about 10 m/s. They conclude that shuttlecock velocity cannot be assessed with such low-frame-rate devices. This bears directly on pixel-displacement speed estimation from 30-60 fps smartphone video.
quote: The difference of velocity between elite and high skilled players is about 10 m.s-1 (Phomsoupha & Laffaye, 2014), whereas the velocity accuracy of a camera at 50 fps is about 5 m.s-1. This showed that it is impossible to assess a badminton shuttlecock velocity with such devices.

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Sci. 4(2):11-19; accepted 2022-11-10; journal web page dated 2025-03-22)
claim: The shuttle slows very quickly after racket contact: the authors report that velocity halves within about 0.05 s of contact (log-decay model V = -9.2 ln(T) + 2.4, T in ms, as printed; the constants look garbled). At 30-60 fps that is only 1.5-3 frames, so frame-differencing tends to miss the true peak, and drag-aware fitting or extrapolation back to the hit frame is needed.
quote: Phomsoupha & Laffaye (2014) showed that the shuttlecock velocity V (in m.s-1) is a logarithmic function of time T (in ms) as follow: V= -9.2 ln(T) +2.4, meaning that the velocity is divided by two times just 0.05 sec after the end of the racket contact.

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Sci. 4(2):11-19; accepted 2022-11-10; journal web page dated 2025-03-22)
claim: Against the 500 Hz high-speed camera, radar correlated at r = 0.917 (the IMU at r = 0.682). Concurrent-validity CVs, 12.5% for radar and 12.1% for the IMU, exceeded the 10% adequacy threshold. About 20% of shots gave no radar reading, partly because the radar is sensitive to placement and tilt.
quote: Also, the Pearson product moment correlation coefficient showed almost perfect correlation between the radar and the high-speed camera measurements for velocity (r= 0.917; p < 0.001); and good correlation between the motion sensor and the high-speed camera measurements (r=0.682; p < 0.001)

published: 2022 (Int. J. Racket Sports Sci. 4(2):11-19; accepted 2022-11-10; journal web page dated 2025-03-22)
claim: The authors fit linear equations to convert high-speed-camera velocity xv into radar-comparable values (0.945xv + 6.703) and IMU-comparable values (0.894xv + 10.273). They report mean smash speeds measured by the high-speed camera of 37.4, 48.6 and 60.1 m/s for novices, intermediates and experts. These give a reference speed range and a way to correct for radar bias.
quote: Linear regression analyses on our data suggests using the following equation to obtain velocity (xv) from the high-speed camera that are comparable to those from the radar (0.945xv + 6.703) and the motion sensor (0.894xv + 10.273) when individuals velocity ranging from novices to experts

published: 2026 (PDF creation date 2026-08-24; the PDF gives no venue or arXiv ID, so it is an author-hosted preprint in ICASSP-style format)
claim: On the public TrackNetV2/V3 shuttlecock dataset, TrackNetV5 (10.09M params) reaches F1 98.47 (Acc 97.37, Prec 99.72, Recall 97.25). It beats TrackNetV3 (11.34M, F1 97.64, Acc 95.98) and TrackNetV4 (11.34M, F1 97.99, Acc 96.58). It also runs at about half their throughput: 60.7 FPS versus about 119 FPS on the same GPU.
quote: TrackNetV5 achieves a leading F1-Score of 98.47, surpassing TrackNetV3 and TrackNetV4. [Table 1:] TrackNetV3 [6] 11.34M 95.98 99.67 95.69 97.64 119.09 / TrackNetV4 [7] 11.34M 96.58 99.56 96.48 97.99 118.81 / TrackNetV5 10.09M 97.37 99.72 97.25 98.47 60.7

published: 2026 (PDF creation date 2026-08-24; the PDF gives no venue or arXiv ID, so it is an author-hosted preprint in ICASSP-style format)
claim: TrackNetV5-Lite (width multiplier 0.5, 2.58M params, about 4.4x fewer than TrackNetV3) reaches F1 98.06 (Acc 96.69). That is still above TrackNetV3 and TrackNetV4. It runs at 135.18 FPS, but the paper measured speed only on a desktop RTX 5080 GPU. It reports no mobile, NPU or TFLite latency, so the paper's claim that it is ready for edge devices is not checked on phone-class hardware such as the Snapdragon 680.
quote: the lightweight TrackNetV5-Lite (2.58M parameters) reaches an F1-Score of 98.06 while running at 135.18 FPS on an RTX 5080

published: 2026 (PDF creation date 2026-08-24; the PDF gives no venue or arXiv ID, so it is an author-hosted preprint in ICASSP-style format)
claim: The paper reports an intermediate variant at width multiplier 0.75: 6.46M params, F1 98.29, Acc 97.07. The authors describe a monotonic accuracy-versus-size/speed trade-off controlled by the width multiplier, so accuracy can be tuned to the device budget.
quote: [Table 3:] 0.75 6.46M 97.07 99.64 96.97 98.29 ... larger α improves accurcy, precision, recall and F1 but increases model size and reduces speed, while smaller α yields a lighter and faster model.

published: 2026 (PDF creation date 2026-08-24; the PDF gives no venue or arXiv ID, so it is an author-hosted preprint in ICASSP-style format)
claim: The evaluation protocol is the standard TrackNet one: 512x288 input, 5-frame input sequences, and a detection counts as a true positive within 4 pixels of ground truth. The numbers are therefore comparable with published TrackNetV2/V3/V4 results on the same dataset, but they say little about sub-pixel or metric accuracy, which matters for speed estimation.
quote: We evaluate TrackNetV5 on the public badminton dataset [5, 6] with frames resized to 512 × 288. The value of T (e.g., sequence length) is set to 5. A prediction is considered a True Positive (TP) if the distance to the ground truth is within 4 pixels [5].

published: 2026 (PDF creation date 2026-08-24; the PDF gives no venue or arXiv ID, so it is an author-hosted preprint in ICASSP-style format)
claim: Over the TrackNetV4 baseline (F1 97.99), the gains are small (about 0.1-0.5 F1 points). In the ablation, adding the R(2+1)D blocks actually lowers F1 from 98.11 to 98.03, and the paper does not explain how the full model reaches 98.47. The method builds on TrackNetV4's motion prompts and does not compare against trajectory rectification/inpainting or against YOLO-family detectors. It dismisses YOLO-family detectors only qualitatively, with no numbers.

FreeTrack (Machine Vision and Applications, vol. 37, art. 167, 2026) reconstructs 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular video with no drag model. It assumes flight between two strikes stays in a vertical 'Motion Plane'. The plane is anchored in time by striking frames and in space by a ground anchor at the midpoint of the player's ankles. Each 2D detection is back-projected through a ray–plane intersection, with no iterative physics fitting.
quote: is strictly confined to a vertical Motion Plane ... without presupposing the trajectory's specific shape or aerodynamic parameters

claim: Against MonoTrack on 96 real sequences (about 17,000 frames, six stroke types), FreeTrack cut landing-point error from 170.9 cm to 7.8 cm on clears, from 103.5 cm to 8.9 cm on smashes and from 97.8 cm to 4.8 cm on flat drives. The authors measured these with a ruler placed in the scene. Landing point is the reference; there is no radar or speed ground truth.
quote: from 170.9 cm to 7.8 cm on Clears ... from 103.5 cm to 8.9 cm on Smashes ... from 97.8 cm to 4.8 cm on Flat Drives

claim: FreeTrack ran 83 times faster than MonoTrack in the same timing scope: 0.705 ms per frame against 46.815 ms per frame. Its cost is light enough for an on-device or real-time 3D stage.
quote: FreeTrack requires only 3.892 s to process the 9 common samples, corresponding to 0.705 ms per frame ... MonoTrack requires 323.597 s, corresponding to 46.815 ms per frame ... FreeTrack is 83.14 times faster than MonoTrack

claim: Camera calibration uses six known 3D–2D court correspondences: the four court corners and the two net-post tops. These give the projection matrix, which supports a court-keypoint/homography approach over pixels-per-meter scaling. On 180 synthetic trajectories generated with aerodynamic drag, the mean 3D error was 16.94 cm.
quote: including four court corners and two net-post tops ... The overall mean error across all trajectories is 16.94 cm

claim: The ankle-based ground anchor is a stated weakness. It can fail on diving saves, jump smashes and falling blocks, where the feet do not mark where the shuttle was struck, and 3D error then grows. The method also assumes negligible crosswind.
quote: ankle-keypoint-based Ground Anchor may deviate from the true contact position and lead to larger 3D reconstruction errors

claim: PnLCalib calibrates a sports-field camera from a single view. A modified HRNetV2-w48 detects field keypoints and line extremities. An initial DLT/RANSAC estimate against a 3D field model is then refined by a non-linear point-and-line (PnL) reprojection optimization. This is a template for court-line keypoint calibration, offered here as an alternative to the app's pixels-per-meter and depth-based calibration.
quote: Particularly, we adopt HRNetv2 [49] as the backbone model for the keypoints and line extremities prediction. ... we propose an optimization-based calibration pipeline that leverages a 3D soccer field model

claim: Adding line-based PnL refinement to keypoint-only calibration raises the Final Score (FS) by 4.3% on SN22-test-center (74.4 to 78.7) and by 7.6% on WC14-test (77.6 to 85.2). This beats the prior best FS of 63.9 and 59.4 on those sets (Mavrogiannis et al.).
quote: by increasing the FS metric by 4.3% on the SN22-test-center dataset and a 7.6% increase on the WC14-test one.

claim: As a homography method on WC14-test, PnLCalib (SV+PnL) reaches mean IoU_whole 93.4 and a mean projection error of 0.60 m, against 92.9 and 0.65 m for the best prior method (Oo et al.). On TS-WorldCup it reaches IoU_whole 96.3 with a 0.23 m mean projection error. These metric-scale errors are on soccer pitches, not badminton courts.
quote: Ours SV + PnL: IoU_part 97.0 / 98.2, IoU_whole 93.4 / 95.5, projection error 0.60 / 0.42 m (WC14-test, mean/median, as reported in results table)

claim: The pipeline is too slow for on-device real-time use as published: about 7 Hz for the plain multi-view model and about 4 Hz average with PnL refinement, on an RTX 2080 Ti GPU. On a phone it would have to run occasionally (calibrate once or rarely) or in cloud post-processing.
quote: the plain MV model achieves 7 Hz ... the inference speed decreases to an average of 4 Hz ... The experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU

claim: The camera model ignores lens distortion (zero skew, known aspect ratio). Extreme-distortion fisheye shots are a stated failure case, a limitation for phone wide-angle or ultra-wide lenses.
quote: Following [22], we assume zero skew and a known pixel aspect ratio. ... i.e., we neglect astigmatism or distortions. ... fisheye shots from inside the goals, where extreme lens distortion makes calibration unable.

published: 2024-09-22 (arXiv v1; the arXiv page says "Research report" and does not mention the ICASSP 2025 venue)
claim: Adding TrackNetV4's motion attention maps to TrackNetV3 improves shuttlecock tracking on the TrackNetV2 shuttlecock dataset. Accuracy rises from 95.7% to 96.4%, recall from 95.4% to 96.3% and F1 from 97.5% to 97.9%. Precision drops slightly, from 99.7% to 99.5%.
quote: Table I (Shuttlecock): 'TrackNetV3 | 95.7 | 99.7 | 95.4 | 97.5' vs 'TrackNetV3 (+Motion) | 96.4 | 99.5 | 96.3 | 97.9' (Acc. / Prec. / Rec. / F1, %); text: 'our method enhances the tracking performance of both TrackNetV2 and V3'

published: 2024-09-22 (arXiv v1; the arXiv page says "Research report" and does not mention the ICASSP 2025 venue)
claim: Adding the motion module to TrackNetV2 on the shuttlecock dataset raises accuracy from 85.6% to 86.6% and F1 from 90.6% to 91.4%. Speed falls only slightly, from 163.3 to 161.1 FPS, so the module adds almost no inference cost.
quote: Table I (Shuttlecock): 'TrackNetV2 | 85.6 | 96.6 | 85.3 | 90.6 | 163.3' vs 'TrackNetV2 (+Motion) | 86.6 | 94.9 | 88.1 | 91.4 | 161.1'; text: 'our motion-aware fusion mechanism still achieves improvements of over 0.8%'

published: 2024-09-22 (arXiv v1; the arXiv page says "Research report" and does not mention the ICASSP 2025 venue)
claim: A general-purpose YOLO detector (YOLOv7) does much worse than heatmap-based TrackNet models on the shuttlecock dataset. It reaches 57.8% accuracy and 68.0% F1, against 85.6% / 90.6% for TrackNetV2 and 95.7% / 97.5% for TrackNetV3.
quote: Table I (Shuttlecock): 'YOLOv7 | 57.8 | 78.5 | 60.0 | 68.0 | -'

published: 2024-09-22 (arXiv v1; the arXiv page says "Research report" and does not mention the ICASSP 2025 venue)
claim: TrackNetV4 is not a new standalone network. It is a lightweight, plug-and-play add-on to existing TrackNet models: frame-differencing maps, modulated by a learnable motion prompt layer, are fused with high-level visual features. It targets cases where TrackNetV1-V3 fail, such as partial occlusion and low visibility.
quote: 'We refer to our lightweight, plug-and-play solution, built on top of the existing TrackNet, as TrackNetV4.' ... TrackNetV1-V3 'often struggle in scenarios with partial occlusion or low visibility.'

published: 2024-09-22 (arXiv v1; the arXiv page says "Research report" and does not mention the ICASSP 2025 venue)
claim: TrackNetV3's reported speed of 15.1 FPS, with or without the motion module, covers the whole script, including data loading and file writing. It cannot be compared directly with TrackNetV2's roughly 160 FPS, so the paper gives no clean inference-latency number for V3 or V4-on-V3.
quote: Table I footnote: '15.1*' with '* Covers the whole script (data loading, file writing, etc.), so it is not directly comparable to the other speeds.'

claim: WASB (1.5M parameters) beats re-implemented TrackNetV2 (11.3M) and MonoTrack (2.9M) on the TrackNetV2 Badminton shuttlecock dataset, using a 4-pixel distance threshold. With oversampling (Step=1), WASB scores F1 93.1, Accuracy 89.0 and AP 91.6. TrackNetV2 scores F1 90.5, Acc 85.6, AP 83.6, and MonoTrack scores F1 90.9, Acc 85.9, AP 84.9. Without oversampling (Step=3), WASB scores F1 91.6, Acc 87.0, AP 88.5.
quote: Table 2 rows (Badminton columns F1/Acc./AP/FPS): "TrackNetV2 [75] 11.3M ... 90.5 85.6 83.6 77.0"; "MonoTrack [50] 2.9M ... 90.9 85.9 84.9 75.5"; "WASB (Ours, Step=3) 1.5M ... 91.6 87.0 88.5 70.4"; "WASB (Ours, Step=1) 1.5M ... 93.1 89.0 91.6 34.3". Caption: "We set the distance threshold τ = 4 [pixel] to compute F1, Accuracy (Acc.) and Average Precision (AP)"

claim: The accuracy gain costs throughput. On badminton, WASB runs at 70.4 FPS without oversampling and 34.3 FPS with Step=1 oversampling, against 77.0 FPS for TrackNetV2. These timings come from a server with 4 V100 GPUs at 288x512 input with 3-frame clips, not from mobile hardware.
quote: Notice that WASB is not the fastest among the methods. However, it can still be processed over 30 FPS on 4 out of 5 datasets, which is reasonable efficiency for real-time inference. ... each image is resized to 288 × 512 ... We performed all the following experiments on an Ubuntu server with 4 V100 GPUs.

claim: WASB deliberately avoids Kalman and particle filters for ball tracking because the authors saw no gain from them. Instead it predicts the next position with a constant-acceleration local motion model and only uses that prediction to discard inconsistent detection candidates. In the ablation, this online tracking added nothing on the Badminton dataset: F1 stayed at 91.6 and AP at 88.5.
quote: Different from classical methods, we do not use filtering algorithms such as Kalman filter ... and particle filter ..., since any performance improvement was not observed with them. ... each technique complementarily ameliorate the SBDT performance with a few exceptions (e.g., online tracking does not contribute on the Soccer and Badminton datasets).

claim: Most of WASB's advantage comes from its high-resolution HRNet backbone with strides removed from the stem. On badminton, the default stem-stride-free design (Fig. 3c) reaches F1 91.6 / AP 88.5, against F1 86.8 / AP 80.3 for the original strided HRNet stem (Fig. 3a). With none of the training or inference tricks, WASB already slightly exceeds the best existing method (F1 91.1 vs 90.9).
quote: Figure 3 (a) 1.5M ... [Badminton] 86.8 80.4 80.3 77.1 ... Figure 3 (c) 1.5M ... 91.6 87.0 88.5 70.4 ... Interestingly, even without any techniques, our method is superior to the best of existing methods (cf. first row in Table 4). This indicates the superiority of our high-resolution feature extraction model to existing approaches.

claim: WASB predicts at most one ball per frame. It was validated only at standard resolutions (HD/FHD) and 25-30 FPS, so its behavior on 60 fps smartphone video is unverified. The Badminton benchmark used here is the TrackNetV2 dataset (1280x720, 30 FPS; 26 training matches and 3 test matches with 12,656 test frames).
quote: our validation is limited to standard frame resolutions (e.g., HD, FHD) and frame rates (e.g., 25-30 FPS). ... Badminton [75] 1280 × 720 30 26 172 78558 11.8 ± 12.2 3 29 12656 12.5 ± 12.9

claim: TrackNetV5 reports a state-of-the-art F1 of 0.9859 and accuracy of 0.9733 on the TrackNetV2 dataset (precision 0.9923, recall 0.9797, 3-frame input at 512x288). It beats TrackNetV2 (F1 0.9677, Acc 0.9396) and TrackNetV4 (F1 0.9581, Acc 0.9224). Most of the gain comes from recall, which rises from 0.9446 for V2 to 0.9797.

TrackNetV5 costs 117.09 GFLOPs and 14.77M parameters, against 112.89 GFLOPs and 11.33M for V2/V4. It runs at about 114 FPS on an NVIDIA T4 server GPU, but no mobile or edge latency is reported. That compute load makes it much better suited to cloud post-processing than to on-device use on a Snapdragon 680-class phone.
quote: with only a 3.7% increase in FLOPs (117.09 G) compared to V4 ... Crucially, it maintains a real-time inference speed of 114 FPS (Table 3, NVIDIA T4: V5 38.12x3 FPS, 117.09 GFLOPs, 14.77M params)

claim: The paper's comparisons include only TrackNetV2 and V4. It gives no numbers for TrackNetV3 (trajectory rectification/inpainting), WASB, MonoTrack or YOLO detectors. It describes V3 qualitatively as heavier and less real-time-friendly, so it does not show that V5 beats TrackNetV3.
quote: Subsequent variants, such as TrackNetV3 ... focused on maximizing accuracy by stacking heavyweight modules (e.g., Inception blocks) ... but at the cost of real-time performance.

claim: TrackNetV5 adds two modules. Motion Direction Decoupling (MDD) keeps signed motion polarity, which V4's absolute frame difference throws away. A Transformer-based Residual-Driven Spatio-Temporal Refinement (R-STR) head predicts a corrective residual intended to recover occluded targets. The occlusion claim rests only on overall false-negative reductions; there is no separate occlusion experiment.
quote: Unlike V4, MDD decomposes temporal dynamics into signed polarity fields ... this Transformer-based module leverages factorized spatio-temporal contexts to estimate a corrective residual, effectively recovering occluded targets.

claim: It is unclear which sport the benchmark covers. The conclusion calls the main dataset the 'TrackNet tennis dataset', while Section 4.1 calls it the 'TrackNetV2 Dataset'. Generalization is shown only on a proprietary LoveAll dataset (V5 F1 0.9878 vs V2 0.9762 and V4 0.9731), so the shuttlecock-specific results cannot be reproduced.
quote: Extensive experiments on the public TrackNet tennis dataset and our proprietary LoveAll dataset

claim: BST (Badminton Stroke-type Transformer) combines player pose, the shuttlecock trajectory and court positions, and beats prior SOTA (TemPose-TF, ST-GCN, BlockGCN, SkateFormer, ProtoGCN) on ShuttleSet, BadmintonDB and TenniSet. On ShuttleSet with 25 merged classes and the clipping strategy, BST-CG-AP scores Acc 0.8322 / Macro-F1 0.8097, against TemPose-TF at 0.8235 / 0.8028. With fixed-width clips, ST-GCN scores only Acc 0.7758 / Macro-F1 0.7352, against 0.8254 / 0.7983 for BST-CG-AP.
quote: To the best of our knowledge, experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art on the largest publicly available badminton video dataset (ShuttleSet), another badminton dataset (BadmintonDB), and a tennis dataset (TenniSet).

claim: On BadmintonDB (18 stroke classes), BST-AP reaches Acc 0.6517 / Macro-F1 0.5799 / Acc-2 0.8628. TemPose-TF scores 0.6199 / 0.5448 / 0.8517 and ST-GCN 0.5602 / 0.4870 / 0.7732. The skeleton-only GCN baseline therefore trails the pose+shuttle Transformer by about 9 points of accuracy.
quote: Nevertheless, our BST series consistently outperforms previous methods.

claim: The BST pipeline gets 2D pose from RTMPose (via MMPose) rather than 3D poses lifted with MotionBERT, because 2D gave better downstream stroke-classification accuracy. It gets 2D shuttle positions from TrackNetV3 (attention variant).
quote: The models we utilized in MMPose are RTMPose [20] for 2D pose estimation and MotionBERT [41] for further 3D pose estimation. ... We choose 2D poses for better downstream accuracy. ... For the shuttlecock trajectories, we utilize the 2D shuttlecock positions generated by TrackNetV3

claim: Adding the shuttle trajectory is the main source of the gains over pose-only models. However, naively adding player court positions to the pose input (PP) lowered some BadmintonDB metrics, so how modalities are fused matters. The strongest results come from clips cut around detected hit frames (the frame when shuttle and racket are in contact or closest), with t set to half the interval between consecutive hit frames.
quote: These results suggest that effectively leveraging ball trajectory is a promising direction for action recognition in racket sports.

claim: BST models are small: BST-CG-AP has about 1.85M parameters, against TemPose-TF 1.71M, ST-GCN 3.08M, SkateFormer 2.38M and ProtoGCN 4.11M. This size suggests on-device deployment is feasible, but the paper reports no inference latency or FLOPs, only training speed on an RTX 4090.
quote: On a NVIDIA RTX 4090 setup, BST-CG-AP trains slightly faster than TemPose-TF

claim: On ShuttleSet stroke recognition (31 classes after merging and splitting by court side; 40 matches split 30/5/5; 33,429 strokes), TemPose-TF-ASF (1.95M params) scores the highest results in the paper: Acc 0.854, Macro-F1 0.761, Acc-2 0.945. BST-CG-AP (1.88M) reaches Acc 0.838 / Macro-F1 0.723 / Acc-2 0.942, and the TemPose-TF baseline (1.71M) reaches 0.835 / 0.742 / 0.927.
quote: TemPose-TF-ASF achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated variants (Table 2: TemPose-TF-ASF 1.95M, Acc 0.854, Macro-F1 0.761, Acc-2 0.945; BST-CG-AP 1.88M, 0.838, 0.723, 0.942)

claim: In the same ShuttleSet benchmark, generic skeleton action-recognition models score lower than badminton-specific models. BlockGCN (1.69M) gets Acc 0.793 / Macro-F1 0.657, SkateFormer (2.38M) gets 0.808 / 0.665, and TemPose-V (1.62M) gets 0.798 / 0.658. This suggests that pose-only GCN or transformer classifiers trail models that fuse pose with shuttle and court data on fine-grained badminton stroke typing.
quote: Table 2: BlockGCN 1.69M Acc 0.793 Macro-F1 0.657; SkateFormer 2.38M Acc 0.808 Macro-F1 0.665; TemPose-V 1.62M Acc 0.798 Macro-F1 0.658

claim: ASF (Adjacent-Stroke Fusion) feeds the stroke types of the preceding and following strokes into the classifier. It works in two stages. In stage 1 the context inputs are set to zero, so the baseline model gives a first prediction. In stage 2 those predicted labels, not ground-truth labels, serve as bidirectional context. Because stage 2 needs the following stroke, this is offline or post-hoc refinement and cannot classify a stroke in real time as it happens.
quote: Preliminary predictions from the baseline model are reused as estimated temporal context. ... Instead of using ground-truth annotations of future strokes, we introduce a Two-Stage Contextual Refinement (TSCR).

claim: ASF works as a plug-in that improves other stroke classifiers as well. Adding it raised BST-CG-AP from Acc 0.838 to 0.843 (Macro-F1 0.723 to 0.729), TemPose-V from 0.798 to 0.814 (Macro-F1 0.658 to 0.701), and BlockGCN from 0.793 to 0.809, at a cost of about 0.24-0.40M extra parameters.
quote: Moreover, integrating ASF into other advanced methods yields notable performance gains. These results demonstrate strong transferability and generalization capability.

claim: The pipeline is multimodal. It combines two-player skeleton joints and bones, shuttlecock trajectories from TrackNetV3, and player court positions from court-line detection (MonoTrack or TennisCourtDetector). The models are small (about 1.6-2.7M params for the main variants), but the paper reports no inference latency or mobile benchmarks.
quote: By explicitly modeling bidirectional temporal stroke dependencies, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing state-of-the-art models.

claim: Morel et al. (VISAPP 2016) compare a novice's sport motion to expert reference motions with a two-level Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) method that aligns the motions both in time and in space. This is an alternative to comparing raw joint angles frame by frame.
quote: we propose an innovative 2-level DTW (Dynamic Time Warping) approach ... to temporally and spatially align the motions and extract the imperfections of the novice's performance for each joints

claim: The method needs only a database of expert motions and no hand-picked features or extra domain knowledge. It reports an error for each joint, and the authors say it is morphology-independent: it is meant to handle differences in body build and style between experts and novices.
quote: Only based on a database of experts' motions and no additional knowledge ... since it is automatic and morphology-independent

claim: The method was tested only on tennis serves, not on badminton strokes. The authors claim it applies to any individual motor skill, but the abstract on this page gives no numbers and no agreement score with coaches or expert raters.
quote: we applied our method on tennis serve ... it can be applied to any individual motor performance

claim: The authors say automatic player scoring is hard because the reference experts and the novices differ in body shape and style. This is why naive per-joint angle comparison against a single pro is unreliable.
quote: the variability of morphologies and styles of both the experts who perform the reference motions

claim: VideoBadminton is a fine-grained badminton action recognition dataset with 18 stroke classes and 7,822 clips (145 minutes) recorded at 60 fps and 1280x960 resolution from 19 university team players. That is far more fine-grained than Ayto's 6-class taxonomy.
quote: It incorporates 18 categories of badminton actions, with a total of 7,822 clips spanning 145 minutes of self-recorded footage. ... Operating at a frame rate of 60fps, the DFK 37AUX273 captured the fast-paced movements inherent in badminton

claim: On the full VideoBadminton dataset (8:1:1 train/val/test split), the RGB-based SlowFast model performed best, with 82.80% Top-1 accuracy and 73.80% mean class accuracy. Video Swin reached 81.99% Top-1, R(2+1)D 79.53% and TimeSformer 73.18%.
quote: SlowFast | 82.80% | 97.54% | 73.80% ... Its Mean Cls Acc of 73.80% is the highest, indicating robustness and versatility in handling various action classes.

claim: Skeleton-based models trailed the best RGB model on the full dataset. PoseC3D reached 80.76% Top-1 and 67.18% mean class accuracy, while ST-GCN reached 74.41% Top-1 and 61.44% mean class accuracy. Pose-only classifiers similar to Ayto's BiLSTM/Transformer on pose sequences lose about 2-8 points of Top-1 compared with RGB video models on this benchmark.

In low-data regimes (the VideoBadminton-10 and VideoBadminton-50 subsets), the skeleton-based ST-GCN beat all RGB video models. On VideoBadminton-50 it led every metric with 60.70% Top-1. This suggests pose-based models are more data-efficient when labeled badminton clips are scarce.
quote: ST-GCN demonstrates the highest Top1 and Top5 Accuracies, suggesting its robustness in smaller datasets. ... In this larger dataset, ST-GCN leads in all metrics, showing its scalability.

claim: MViT-V2 failed on VideoBadminton, reaching only 14.23% Top-1 and 10.76% mean class accuracy. Not every state-of-the-art general video transformer transfers to fine-grained badminton stroke recognition.
quote: MViT-V2 displays significant limitations with notably lower scores across all metrics, suggesting major challenges in action recognition.

claim: On the RacketVision badminton split, a multi-sport TrackNetV3 with background-median input and 4-frame context scored best: precision 0.915, recall 0.865, mean distance error 1.54 px and mAP@50 83.1. The general-purpose detectors scored lower. YOLO11 (single frame) reached P 0.858, R 0.548, MDE 29.3 px, mAP 72.1, and RTMDet reached P 0.801, R 0.721, MDE 38.2 px, mAP 64.2. WASB reached P 0.907, R 0.803, MDE 4.03 px, mAP 58.7. So heatmap trackers localize the shuttle about 10-20x more precisely than YOLO11 or RTMDet. Caveat: the footage is 1080p professional broadcast with sparse 20% frame annotation, not smartphone video.
quote: The best overall results in our benchmark are achieved by MS-TrackNetV3 with 4 frames. [Table 3, Badminton: YOLO11 0.858 0.548 29.3 72.1; WASB 0.907 0.803 4.03 58.7; MS-TrackNetV3 BM #F=4 0.915 0.865 1.54 83.1]

claim: Adding a per-clip background median frame as extra input to single-frame TrackNetV3 cut the mean shuttle localization error by 54.8% on badminton (MDE 7.39 px down to 3.34 px). It also raised badminton mAP from 57.8 to 67.7.
quote: comparing TrackNetV3 (#F=1) with and without BM, background modeling reduces MDE by a remarkable 54.0% for Table Tennis, 61.4% for Tennis, and 54.8% for Badminton.

claim: Training the ball tracker on badminton, tennis and table tennis together raised badminton mAP@50 from 72.5 (best single-sport TrackNetV3) to 83.1. Single-sport models sometimes kept a slight edge in pinpoint localization.
quote: the MS model boosts mAP by a significant 19.2% in Tennis (81.9 vs. 68.7) and 14.6% in Badminton (83.1 vs. 72.5).

claim: For predicting where the shuttle goes next from its 2D history, simply concatenating racket-pose features made LSTM and Transformer predictors worse than ball-only models. Cross-attention fusion of racket pose with an LSTM was best overall, but its gain on badminton was small. Short-horizon ADE went from 37.5 to 37.0 px, and long-horizon ADE/FDE went from 118.7/194.7 to 114.6/187.6 px. The Transformer predictors did worse than the LSTMs.
quote: simply concatenating racket pose features consistently leads to worse performance than the ball-only baseline for both LSTM and Transformer backbones... In Short Badminton, ADE improves from 37.5 to 37.0.

claim: A top-down RTMPose model (with an RTMDet detector) trained on all three sports estimated 5-keypoint badminton racket pose at PCK@0.2 88.5%, MPJPE 5.00 px and mOKS 0.668. Its accuracy was above 97% for the top, bottom and handle keypoints but only about 75% for the left and right side keypoints, because of grip occlusion and motion blur.
quote: badminton excels in pose quality metrics with the lowest MPJPE (5.00px) and highest mOKS (0.668), demonstrating the effectiveness of cross-sport knowledge transfer.

claim: The preprint (actual title: 'Badminton Technical Movement Evaluation: A New Benchmark and Baseline Model', Song et al., Qilu Normal Univ. / Aerospace Information Technology Univ.) introduces a coach-reference technique-scoring benchmark. It has 7,200 smartphone-captured clips of 10 basic strokes from 5 professional coaches and 67 university students. Students are scored on a 100-point scale by several coaches; the highest and lowest scores are dropped and the rest averaged. The stroke set is Forehand/Backhand Clear, Forehand/Backhand Serve, Forehand/Backhand Lift, Forehand/Backhand Net Drop and Forehand/Backhand Drive. It has no smash, so it does not line up with Ayto's 6 classes.
quote: The dataset contains 7,200 smartphone-captured video clips covering 10 fundamental badminton strokes, collected from 5 professional coaches and 67 university students across multiple real-world scenarios. Student performances are annotated on a 100-point scale by expert coaches using a multi-rater scoring protocol.

claim: The learned exemplar-vs-student baseline only agrees moderately with expert coach scores. On a held-out test set of 14 students (split by subject, 53 train / 14 test) it gets MAE 7.47, RMSE 9.09, SRCC 0.56, PLCC 0.58, Acc5 (error within 5 points) 38% and Acc10 (within 10 points) 73%. The paper reports no other baseline, such as DTW or joint-angle comparison, to measure these numbers against.
quote: Experimental results on the test set show that the proposed baseline achieves promising performance, with a reported MAE of 7.47, SRCC of 0.56, PLCC of 0.58, and Acc10 of 73%.

claim: The scoring model works on raw RGB, not pose, and does no explicit temporal alignment such as DTW. It encodes each frame with a pretrained ViT, using only T=8 sampled frames at 224x224. It fuses frames with self-attention plus average pooling, compares coach and student embeddings by subtraction plus bilinear pooling, and regresses a score with an RMSE loss. Each student clip is scored against all 5 coach templates, and the highest and lowest predictions are dropped before averaging.
quote: we first compute the overall discrepancy between the exemplar and student features via a subtraction operation

claim: Accuracy varies a lot by stroke. Backhand Drive is the best (SRCC 0.75, PLCC 0.75, MAE 6.04, Acc10 82%) and Backhand Serve is also strong (SRCC 0.68). The overhead Forehand Clear is the worst (SRCC 0.32, PLCC 0.34, MAE 8.90, Acc10 64%), followed by Forehand Serve (SRCC 0.34, PLCC 0.38). This suggests that fast overhead strokes are the hardest to grade from the 8-frame RGB representation.
quote: In contrast, the prediction performance on the remaining 2 strokes, namely Forehand Clear and Forehand Serve, is relatively inferior.

claim: The data was recorded on smartphones, either on a tripod or handheld, and students performed strokes in places other than courts, such as dormitories and teaching buildings. The dataset is not publicly released and is available only on request. This makes it closer to Ayto's casual phone-capture setting but harder to reproduce.
quote: Therefore, we require students to perform the technical movements in different scenarios, including dormitories and teaching buildings, rather than being limited to badminton courts only.

claim: On ShuttleSet with 100 training clips, the metric is F1evt at a strict ±1-frame tolerance on racket-shuttle contact frames across 36 classes. UMEG-Net, a skeleton + shuttle + court graph model, reaches 49.2 F1evt and 64.0 Edit. Baselines score lower: BlockGCN 47.1/59.4, F3ED 44.1/55.1, E2E-Spot 800MF 42.7/54.6. The distilled RGB variant (UMEG-Net distill) reaches 59.1 F1evt and 69.0 Edit.
quote: "Each shot is annotated with the exact racket–shuttle contact frame and its event type (36 categories)." ... "Unless otherwise specified, we use a strict tolerance of δ=1 frame" (Table 1, ShuttleSet, 100-clip: E2E-Spot 800MF 42.7/54.6; F3ED 44.1/55.1; BlockGCN 47.1/59.4; UMEG-Net 49.2/64.0; UMEG-Net distill 59.1/69.0)

claim: UMEG-Net combines human skeletons, the shuttle/ball and court-corner keypoints in one graph. It uses 2.2M parameters, the fewest of the compared baselines. That size suits on-device learned hit-frame detection on top of an existing pose + shuttle pipeline. The paper reports no inference latency or FLOPs.
quote: "UMEG-Net integrates human skeletons and sport-specific object keypoints into a unified graph" ... "with the fewest parameters (2.2M) among all baselines."

claim: Across five fine-grained sports datasets, UMEG-Net improves F1 by 1.3-5.5% and Edit score by 1.3-16.4%. Distilling the keypoint-graph teacher into a VideoMAEv2 RGB student (listed at 67.8M parameters) adds an average 5.8% F1 and 6.7% Edit. That student is a cloud-scale option rather than an on-device one.
quote: "improving F1 scores by 1.3% to 5.5% and edit scores by 1.3% to 16.4%" ... "achieves an additional average gain of 5.8% in F1 score and 6.7% in edit score"

claim: The ShuttleSet pipeline relies on upstream detectors: TrackNetV3 for shuttle tracking, YOLOv8 player detection filtered to players whose feet are inside the court, and a separate court-corner detector. The authors acknowledge that keypoint-based event spotting degrades when those detections are unreliable in fast-moving sports.
quote: "shuttlecock tracking is performed with TrackNetV3" ... "keypoint-based approaches depend on accurate detections, which are often unreliable in fast-moving sports"

claim: Under full supervision (not few-shot), UMEG-Net does not beat all baselines on every dataset. It is better on only 3 of the 5 evaluated datasets, so its advantage is mainly in the low-label regime.
quote: "It shows better performance in 3 out of 5 datasets."

published: 2023 (ICCV 2023; arXiv 2210.06551 v1 12 Oct 2022, v5 camera-ready 14 Aug 2023). The CVF link returned 403, so the content was read from the identical arXiv v5 PDF.
claim: MotionBERT's DSTformer (finetuned from pretraining) reaches 37.5 mm MPJPE on Human3.6M from detected 2D keypoints (Stacked Hourglass) with a 243-frame clip, beating MixSTE (39.8 mm, CVPR'22) and P-STMO (42.1 mm). With ground-truth 2D input it reaches 16.9 mm, against 21.6 mm for MixSTE. This makes it the strongest 2D-to-3D lifting baseline for monocular 3D pose as of 2023.
quote: Table 1 (Top, detected 2D): 'Ours (finetune) 243 ... Avg 37.5' vs 'MixSTE CVPR'22 243 ... 39.8'; (Middle, GT 2D): 'Ours (finetune) 243 ... 16.9' vs 'MixSTE 243 ... 21.6'. Text: 'As shown in Table 1 (middle), our models significantly outperform all the previous approaches.'

published: 2023 (ICCV 2023; arXiv 2210.06551 v1 12 Oct 2022, v5 camera-ready 14 Aug 2023). The CVF link returned 403, so the content was read from the identical arXiv v5 PDF.
claim: MotionBERT also produces smoother 3D motion. Its mean per-joint velocity error (MPJVE) on Human3.6M with detected 2D input is 1.7 mm, against 2.3 mm for MixSTE, 3.1 mm for PoseFormer and 3.0 mm for VideoPose3D. A learned temporal lifter therefore reduces jitter, which is the same problem that EMA, One-Euro or SmoothNet smoothing targets.
quote: 'Table 1 (bottom) shows that both of our models also surpass previous works in terms of MPJVE, implying better temporal coherence.' Table 1 (Bottom): 'Ours (finetune) 243 ... 1.7'; 'MixSTE ... 2.3'; 'PoseFormer ... 3.1'

published: 2023 (ICCV 2023; arXiv 2210.06551 v1 12 Oct 2022, v5 camera-ready 14 Aug 2023). The CVF link returned 403, so the content was read from the identical arXiv v5 PDF.
claim: When the pretrained encoder is finetuned for skeleton-based action recognition, it reaches 93.0% (X-Sub) and 97.2% (X-View) top-1 accuracy on NTU-RGB+D 60, using HRNet 2D joints only. On one-shot recognition on NTU-RGB+D-120 it scores 67.4%, against 54.2% for the previous best (Skeleton-DML). This shows that the pretrained motion representations transfer well to classification tasks with few labels, such as badminton stroke types.
quote: 'We perform one-shot action recognition using 1-nearest-neighbor with the exemplars and achieve 67.4% top-1 accuracy.' Table 2: 'Ours (finetune) 93.0 97.2'; 'Skeleton-DML [80] 54.2'; 'Ours (finetune) 67.4'

published: 2023 (ICCV 2023; arXiv 2210.06551 v1 12 Oct 2022, v5 camera-ready 14 Aug 2023). The CVF link returned 403, so the content was read from the identical arXiv v5 PDF.
claim: The model is a large Transformer that works on long temporal windows. Its configuration is depth 5, 8 heads and 512-dimensional features, pretrained on 243-frame sequences (about 4-8 s at 30-60 fps). The paper reports no parameter count, FLOPs or mobile latency. Running it on a Snapdragon 680-class device would therefore need distillation or shorter windows; the paper does not validate this, so it is best treated as a cloud post-processing option.
quote: 'We implement the proposed motion encoder DSTformer with depth N = 5, number of heads h = 8, feature size Cf = 512, embedding size Ce = 512. For pretraining, we use sequence length T = 243.'

published: 2023 (ICCV 2023; arXiv 2210.06551 v1 12 Oct 2022, v5 camera-ready 14 Aug 2023). The CVF link returned 403, so the content was read from the identical arXiv v5 PDF.
claim: A frozen pretrained backbone with only a task head still performs well: 40.3 mm MPJPE and 87.3% NTU X-View accuracy, against 404.4 mm and 47.6% for a randomly initialised frozen backbone. This lets one shared encoder serve several tasks (3D pose, stroke classification). The stated limitation is that the representation covers single-person skeletons only and ignores appearance and interactions, such as the racket or shuttle.
quote: 'Pretraining and partial finetuning make it possible for all the downstream tasks to share the same backbone, significantly reducing computation overhead' ... 'The primary limitation of this work lies in its focus on single-person skeleton sequences, which results in the motion representation being insensitive to factors such as appearance, surroundings, and interactions.'

claim: Hit detection from the shuttle trajectory alone (original TrackNet with peak and direction identification) has high recall but low precision: P=0.588, R=0.936, F1=0.723 at temporal IoU 0.5 on BWF match videos. Combining it with YOLOv7 swing detection through a rule-based Shot Refinement Algorithm (SRA) raises this to P=0.897, R=0.913, F1=0.905. The abstract calls the 0.897 figure 'accuracy', but Table 1 labels it precision.
quote: Our proposed method achieves an accuracy of 89.7%, a recall rate of 91.3%, and an F1 rate of 90.5% in 69 matches, with 1582 rallies of the Badminton World Federation (BWF) match videos. This is a significant improvement compared to the use of TrackNet alone, which yields 58.8% accuracy, 93.6% recall, and 72.3% F1 score.

claim: The fused hit detector uses two learned visual cues: TrackNet (v1) for the shuttle trajectory and a YOLOv7 detector, trained on manually labeled hit actions, that finds which player is swinging. Each cue is used to remove the other's false detections. This shows that fusing a learned swing detector with the trajectory beats peak or threshold heuristics alone, which bears directly on replacing wrist-velocity peak thresholding.
quote: Second, the YOLOv7 model is used to identify whether the player is swinging. As both TrackNet and YOLOv7 may have detection misses and false detections, this study proposes a shot refinement algorithm to obtain the correct hitting moment.

claim: Hit-frame localization falls off sharply under stricter temporal IoU. At t-IoU 0.85, the best fused method (Tuned+SRA) gets only F1=0.472, and at t-IoU 0.95 it gets F1=0.270. TrackNet alone gets 0.162 and 0.056 at the same thresholds.
quote: the trajectory-based method only yielded a precision of 0.588, a recall rate of 0.936, and an F1 score of 0.723

claim: Shot-type classification uses XGBoost on seven hand-crafted features: both players' ankle court positions, shuttle flight duration, and shuttle displacement (dx, dy), over 7 classes (clear, drive, smash, net, drop, lift, push). Accuracy is only 72.1%, 65.4% and 54.1% at the three thresholds (54.1% at t-IoU 0.5, 72.1% at 0.95). This is a weak non-deep baseline against pose-sequence models such as BST or GCN-based classifiers.
quote: Furthermore, the accuracy of shot type classification at three different thresholds is 72.1%, 65.4%, and 54.1%.

claim: The extra YOLOv7 model raises processing time about 5x compared with trajectory-only hit detection (about 0.032 s to about 0.175 s in Table 1, on an RTX 3080Ti desktop). The single monocular viewpoint is named as a limitation, and 3D shuttle and ankle coordinates are proposed as future work. This bears on whether the method can run on a mid-range phone.
quote: Because the proposed method includes an additional YOLO model, the overall processing time is increased.

claim: MonoTrack's 2D shuttle tracker reaches 88.6% tracking accuracy on the TrackNetV2-based dataset, up from 84.0% for TrackNetV2, while using about a quarter of the parameters (2.9M vs 11.3M). This makes it a stronger and lighter option than the app's current TrackNetV2 heatmap tracker.
quote: 88.6% accuracy from 84.0% in the original ... 2.9M parameters in our model versus 11.3M parameters

claim: MonoTrack's learned hit detector (HitNet, about 16K parameters) plus a trajectory-aware optimization step reaches 89.7% accuracy, 94.9% precision, 94.3% recall and F1 0.946 for hit/shot segmentation. That is more than 35% better than a naive baseline, and the detector runs at several thousand frames per second.
quote: our model offers a substantial (>35%) accuracy improvement of the hit detection over the naive model ... can reach 86.3% accuracy [before optimization]

claim: MonoTrack's improved court-line detection raises the court detection success rate (IoU > 0.8) from 73.9% to 85.5%, with average IoU of 0.97 (vs 0.96), and cuts average detection time by a factor of 40. This is relevant to replacing pixels-per-meter calibration with court homography.
quote: increases the success rate of court detection from 73.9% to 85.5% ... decreased the average detection time by a factor of 40

claim: MonoTrack reconstructs 3D shuttle trajectories from a single camera by fitting a physics model (gravity plus quadratic air drag, with the drag coefficient fitted per shot) together with court and shot-placement priors. On synthetic data the priors cut 3D error from 14.9 cm to 8.0 cm. On real video the worst end-to-end reprojection error was 37.1 px (about 5%).
quote: adding the priors improves the error from 14.9 cm to 8.0 cm ... The highest error is 37.1 pixels, or about 5%

claim: MonoTrack calls itself the first complete end-to-end system for extracting and segmenting 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular badminton video. It was trained and evaluated on 77k annotated frames from 26 singles matches (TrackNetV2 base), with a test set of about 12k frames from 3 matches, plus 40 extra matches labeled for court detection.
quote: integrates badminton domain knowledge such as court dimension, shot placement, physical laws of motion ... 77k annotated frames from 26 unique singles matches

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1; v2 revised 2025-10-24, formatted as IEEE Transactions on Image Processing)
claim: HP-MCoRe scores technique against a reference performance instead of comparing joint angles one by one. It splits the query video and an exemplar video into sub-action phases (for diving: take-off, flight, entry) and predicts a relative score for each phase. Those phase scores are added to the exemplar's known score to give the final score. This is a learned, phase-aligned way to compare against an exemplar, and it could replace per-joint angle comparison against a pro.
quote: our proposed method begins by segmenting both the query and exemplar videos into sub-actions ... the relative scores of each sub-action are summed with the ground truth score S e of the exemplar video to compute the predicted score

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1; v2 revised 2025-10-24, formatted as IEEE Transactions on Image Processing)
claim: On FineDiving, HP-MCoRe reports a Spearman correlation (SRCC) of 0.9383 and RL2 (x100) of 0.269 when dive numbers are used, and 0.9041 / 0.411 without them. The baselines in the same table, with dive numbers, are TSA at 0.9203, MCoRe at 0.9232, T2CR at 0.9275 and PECoP at 0.9315.
quote: our method achieved an SRCC of 0.9041 and an RL2 of 0.411 without using dive numbers. When dive numbers are incorporated, the SRCC improves to 0.9383 and the RL2 reduces to 0.269.

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1; v2 revised 2025-10-24, formatted as IEEE Transactions on Image Processing)
claim: The skeleton features alone are much weaker than when fused with video. The hierarchical skeletal encoder (built on HD-GCN) used by itself reaches only 0.6847 SRCC on FineDiving, but adding it to the visual encoders raises SRCC by 3.57% over the visual-only baseline. This suggests that comparing quality from pose alone loses information that appearance cues carry.
quote: utilizing the HSE alone results in inferior performance, with an SRCC of only 0.6847. It is attributed to the absence of some crucial visual information

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1; v2 revised 2025-10-24, formatted as IEEE Transactions on Image Processing)
claim: The authors argue that cutting videos into fixed-length clips breaks the continuity of sub-actions. Their learned procedure-segmentation network for phase boundaries reaches AIoU@0.5/0.75 of 98.17/93.68 on FineDiving without dive numbers, against 80.71/30.17 for TSA. With dive numbers it reaches 99.07/97.96, against 98.26/79.17 for MCoRe. This is learned phase alignment, an alternative to DTW-style temporal alignment. The paper itself does not evaluate DTW.
quote: existing methods focus on segmenting the video into fixed frames, which disrupts the temporal continuity of sub-actions resulting in unavoidable prediction errors

published: 2025-01-07 (arXiv v1; v2 revised 2025-10-24, formatted as IEEE Transactions on Image Processing)
claim: The full model is a heavy server-class network: about 138.1 GFLOPs and 16.8M parameters, using an I3D video backbone plus HD-GCN. It reaches 0.9516 SRCC on MTL-AQA (with difficulty labels), close to TPT's 0.9552, which needs 557.64 GFLOPs. At this cost it is cloud post-processing only and not feasible on-device on mid-range phones.
quote: our method achieves lower GFLOPs and fewer parameters than state-of-the-art models such as TPT and TSA, while maintaining competitive performance.

claim: JEANIE extends soft-DTW (a differentiable DTW) to align two 3D skeleton sequences jointly over time and simulated camera viewpoint. Plain DTW and soft-DTW align only in time. JEANIE takes the soft-minimum over warping paths in a 4D temporal-viewpoint grid, with each step limited to adjacent time blocks and adjacent views ("1-max shift"). For Ayto's stage 7 (pro technique comparison), this is a published improvement over plain DTW or soft-DTW for comparing a user's motion with a pro's when the two clips were shot from different camera angles.
quote: JEANIE selects the smallest distance among matching paths with different temporal-viewpoint warping patterns, an advantage over DTW which only performs temporal alignment.

claim: In supervised few-shot action recognition on NTU-60 with an S2GC backbone, soft-DTW (temporal alignment only) reaches 53.7-67.8% accuracy for 10-50 training classes. The best JEANIE variant (+crossval +Transformer) reaches 65.0-80.0% on the same settings. Two-axis viewpoint alignment alone adds 5-8% over simply concatenating viewpoints.
quote: Table 5 (Sup.) shows that using the viewpoint alignment simultaneously in two dimensions, x and y for Euler angles, or azimuth and altitude the stereo projection geometry (CamVPC), improves the performance by 5–8%

claim: On the UWA3D Multiview Activity II cross-view benchmark (supervised, S2GC backbone), mean accuracy is 56.7% with soft-DTW, 59.5% with Free Viewpoint Matching and 63.7% with JEANIE. In the unsupervised setting, JEANIE's gain over soft-DTW is about 10%. On NTU-120 (100 training classes), JEANIE beats SL-DML by 6.1% and Skeleton-DML by 2.8%.
quote: Table 8 (Unsup.) shows that the biggest improvement is obtained when using unsupervised JEANIE on UWA3D Multiview Activity II dataset, with 10% performance gain.

claim: JEANIE's viewpoint alignment needs 3D skeletons and was not evaluated on 2D keypoints. On Kinetics-skeleton (YouTube video, including phone footage), 3D skeletons beat 2D by 3-4%, but camera-viewpoint simulation added only about 0.3% over Euler-angle rotation because it becomes unreliable on such footage. For a single-phone-camera app, this means 3D pose lifting would be needed before JEANIE-style view-invariant comparison, and the viewpoint gains seen on lab datasets may shrink on in-the-wild video.
quote: the camera viewpoint simulation becomes unreliable especially when videos are captured by multiple different devices, e.g., camera and mobile phone.

claim: JEANIE's encoder is small (0.25-0.5M parameters, versus 0.47M+24M for VA-RNN+VA-CNN), but the full pipeline is heavy to train and preprocess. Viewpoint generation took 1.6h of non-optimized CPU preprocessing, and parallel training took 44h on 4 GPUs. On MSRAction3D, the supervised pipeline took about 1.95 s per 10 episodes. All benchmarks are few-shot action recognition, not technique-similarity scoring. Applying it to on-device pro comparison would therefore require adaptation, and its latency on a phone is not shown.
quote: Training JEANIEpar with 4 Titan RTX 2090 took 44h, the total inference was 48s.
